messages.subject_clean: Path Analysis, Total score and Direct and Indirect effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

There is another question, I was hoping someone could help me with. When I calculate the total score. How do I know, how to include which variables in the total calculation?
For example, I was interested in calculating the direct and indirect effects. So I used this calculation. But I wasn't sure, if I should add the b+d to calculate the total score.

All best,

Nina

modelstrange6 <- '
# latent variable definitions
#psychological functioning
selfregulation =~ PS2 + PS3 + PS4 + PS7 + PS8 + PS10 + PS14
na =~ PS5 + PS9 + PS11 + PS18 + PS19
lowresilience =~ rPS6 + rPS12 + rPS15 + rPS16 + rPS20
#sleep
quantity =~ ZSP_DDPOZ6 + ZSP_PDPOZ6 + ZPSPDEPR
quality =~ ZPSPNESP1 + ZPSPNESP2 + ZPSPNESP3 + ZPSPMS
latency =~ ZPSPLAT + ZPSPLAT2

#outcomes
medicalerr =~  MN_IZC + MN_P
safetycomp =~ VAR_D + VAR_IND

sleep =~ quantity + 1*quality + latency
psychf =~ 1*selfregulation + lowresilience + na

# regressions
psychf ~ a*sleep
medicalerr ~ b*psychf + c*sleep
safetycomp ~ d*psychf + e*sleep

#covariances
medicalerr ~~ safetycomp
PS7 ~~ PS8
PS2 ~~ PS4
rPS6 ~~ rPS20
PS5 ~~ PS19
PS18 ~~ PS19
PS7 ~~ PS10

ab:= a*b
ac:= a*d
total:= a*b+a*d+c+e + b + d
'

messages.subject: Re: script and data related to the post about bifactors and lavaan::: sam/FSR+Croon
messages.subject_clean: script and data related to the post about bifactors and lavaan::: sam/FSR+Croon
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nikola,

On 8/31/20 10:53 PM, Nikola Ćirović wrote:
> Namely, the global SAM that you have found to be the only to work for my
> model with bifactors seem to produce a bad fit (which is fair), however,
> I have noticed that the global SAM-obtained chi-square and df correspond
> to those I get by applying SEM.

That is correct. 'global' SAM still estimates the parameters in 2 steps:
first the measurement part, then (keep the measurement part fixed) the
structural part. To evaluate the model, it uses the same chi-square test
statistic (technically, it is just an approximation) as regular sem.

If you get a 'bad' fit, it is very likely that this is due to some of
the measurement models. This is 'global' fit: both the measurement and
structural part of the model are evaluated together (just like in
regular sem).

> However, the reviewer that suggested FSR+Croon to me made his
> suggestion based on the assumption that this will allow me to test the
> fit of the model that takes only structural relations in consideration

If this is what you really want, then you can use fit the CFA part of
the model (all latent variables in the model, but without the
'structural' part). Then you can extract the variance/covariance matrix
of the latent variables, using

COV <- lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

and then you can fit the structural part only using 'COV' as the input
covariance matrix. The standard errors will be underestimated, but it
will give you a good sense of the fit of the structural part (only). In
other words, you don't need FSR/SAM for this.

> More importantly, when I apply local SAM to the
> model where group-specific factors are taken out (so I have ordinary
> unidimensional factors for both mediator and outcome instead of the
> bifactors) - the df is 5 and fit is (no surprise) good. This would allow
> me to test the fit of the simplified version of my model and answer the
> review. As I have no publication to rely on, I would be greatly thankful
> if you told me if I am basing anything here on a wrong assumption on how
> local SAM works.

Local SAM is really (almost) identical to FSR+Croon, so you can refer to
the papers of Devlieger et.al <http://et.al>.

> My question would, in short be, can I use the local SAM
> as I have described (I get the model with 5 df and only the structural
> paths and covariances estimated), call this FSR + Croon and cite
> Devlieger & Rosseel, 2017 (and Devlieger, Mayer, & Rosseel, 2016)?

Yes.

> Also, I see that standard errors in local SAM
> differ when I use MLR as opposed to ML (by a small bit) and so I was
> wondering if this is relevant.

The MLR part if only used for the 'first step' (the CFA part of the
model). This may indeed lead to small changes, but usually not much.

Yves.

I had a problem with computing standard error in running SEM(cross-lagged effect model).
The following was my code:
  model2009 <-'
    #factor analysis(latent variables)
    internal1 =~1*INFLU1+COMPLEX1
    institution1 =~ 1*PARTY1+ELECTION1+CONGRESS1
    internal2 =~1*INFLU2+COMPLEX2
    institution2 =~ 1*PARTY2+ELECTION2+CONGRESS2

   #unique variances of observed variables
    INFLU1~~INFLU1; COMPLEX1~~COMPLEX1; PARTY1~~PARTY1;                 ELECTION1~~ELECTION1; CONGRESS1~~CONGRESS1
    INFLU2~~INFLU2; COMPLEX2~~COMPLEX2; PARTY2~~PARTY2;       ELECTION2~~ELECTION2; CONGRESS2~~CONGRESS2

   #structural equation
    internal2~internal1+institution1;
    institution2~internal1+institution1;

   #covariances between latent variables
    internal1~~institution1; internal2~~institution2; internal1~~internal1;         institution1~~institution1; internal2~~internal2; institution2~~institution2v
'

Thanks to community member's advice, I found not confining the coefficient disturbed identifying the models.
So I improved the model part as following:
  internal1 =~1*INFLU1+a*COMPLEX1
  institution1 =~ 1*PARTY1+b*ELECTION1+c*CONGRESS1
  internal2 =~1*INFLU2+a*COMPLEX2
  institution2 =~ 1*PARTY2+b*ELECTION2+c*CONGRESS2

But I still have an error message.
The error message is
  Gamma.g * tcrossprod(a1) でerror:  適切な配列ではありません (in English; The arrangement is not proper.)

How should I solve this?
Best wishes,
 Ashu

thanks for the fast reply, which I did not expect and therefore didn`t notice before I left my office for some weeks.

Yes, I am using a robust estimator, i.e. WLSMV, as I treat my items (5 point-Likert) as categorical.

Following your advice, I tried ML with an example dataset from:
Pendergast et al. (2017). Measurement equivalence: A non-technical primer on categorical multi-group confirmatory factor analysis in school psychology,
Journal of School Psychology, 60, 65–82 (http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2016.11.002).

I used their example model (see Mplus input), which I wrote in lavaan as:

model <- ' F1 =~ ss1r + ss2 + ss3r + ss4r + ss5 + ss6r
           F2 =~ sa7 + sa8 + sa9 + sa10r + sa12

        ss1r ~~ ss3r
        ss1r ~~ ss4r
        ss1r ~~ ss6r
        ss3r ~~ ss4r
        ss3r ~~ ss6r
        ss4r ~~ ss6r
        ss6r ~~ sa10r'
(the correlated residuals are relevant for me as I also have some in my own data/model..)

To make it reproducible I attach the data and Mplus input file here.

>From my first checks it seems that indeed all values (MI, EPC, power, NCP) are identical to Mplus with plain ML.
However, using MLR, small deviations are noticeable.
The stronger deviations arise with estimator WLS, again even more intense using WLSMV, which is the scenario I first encountered this issue.
Thus, it would be nice to have some explanation and/or solution for it that does also apply to categorical items (WLS/WLSMV) and not only to ML.

I`m curiuos about your "findings" for this case... ;)
Thx in advance & kind regards,
Jan

messages.subject: Re: Warning that solution not found with results
messages.subject_clean: Warning that solution not found with results
messages.body_plain:
Indeed, this is confusing. This is 'new' in 0.6-7: if the first attempt
to estimate the parameters fails, lavaan tries again. In fact, 4
attempts are done (2 different starting values, 2 different ways to
handle the scale of the data). In your case, the first two attempts
failed, producing two warnings, but the third one succeeded.

So you can ignore the warnings. In a future update, they will no longer
be shown (if one of the attempts succeeded).

In your setting, the initial starting values did not work. But the
'simple' ones do work:

fit <- sem(Model1, sample.cov = S_LD, estimator = "DWLS", WLS.V =
W_Reorder, sample.nobs = 2,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, verbose = TRUE, start = "simple")

producing no warning.

Yves.

messages.subject: Factor scores for numerical vs. ordinal indicators in multi-group analysis (ME/I)
messages.subject_clean: Factor scores for numerical vs. ordinal indicators in multi-group analysis (ME/I)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

first, thanks to all involved in the development of the lavaan and semTools packages which make SEM analyses accessible to mere applied researchers like me who are not fluent in math and/or "hardcore R".

My current task involves testing for group differences on a scale based on rating items after establishing measurement invariance. Since I admittedly do not know how to do this directly in lavaan, my idea was to get factor scores for the scalar invariance model via lavPredict and use these for the group comparisons.

What puzzles me is that this seems to work very well when declaring the items as numerical data but not when declaring them as ordinal data. A mock dataset "fdat" with just two groups is attached.

# R code
model <- 'factor =~ i1 + i2 + i3 + i4 + i5 + i6'

scalinv.n <- cfa (model, data = fdat, estimator = "MLM", group = "grp", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
scalinv.o <- cfa(model, data = fdat, ordered = T, group = "grp", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))

facsco <- data.frame(cbind(fdat$rid[order(fdat$rid)], fdat$grp[order(fdat$rid)],
lavPredict(scalinv.n, type="lv", method="regression", assemble=T, label=T)[order(fdat$rid),],
lavPredict(scalinv.o, type="lv", method="EBM", assemble=T, label=T)[order(fdat$rid),]))
#

>From summary(scalinv.n):
Group 2 [a]:
Intercepts:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    factor           -0.442    0.080   -5.530    0.000

This corresponds exactly to the mean difference between the two groups in "facsco" for the lavPredict variable created from scalinv.n (even though the lavPredict-based standard error for the mean difference is a bit smaller).

>From summary(scalinv.o):
Group 2 [a]:
Intercepts:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    factor           -0.350    0.063   -5.530    0.000

By contrast, the mean difference between the two groups in "facsco" for the lavPredict variable created from scalinv.o is a mere -0.108.

Any enlightenment or even hints on how to get factor scores for (grouped) ordinal data where the estimated intercept difference corresponds to the mean difference for the factor scores like for the ML-based approach (preferably without too much advanced wizardry involved) would be highly appreciated.

Best regards and thanks,
Michael

messages.subject_clean: Factor scores for numerical vs. ordinal indicators in multi-group analysis (ME/I)
messages.body_plain:
Michael,

That's not something you can expect.

When you declare data as ordered, you take away the meaning of the numbers attached to them. A variable with possible values 1, 2, 3, 4 and one with values -93, 0, 5, 10000 are treated the same: four sequential bins. So referring to the "mean" of ordered variables has no meaning.

I'm pretty certain, unless instructed otherwise, lavaan treats cfa() factors with ordered indicators as having a latent mean of 0 and variance of 1, regardless of the numeric labels of the indicators, because they really should be treated just as labels. Think of it this way: there's no in-principle reason ordinal methods couldn't be applied to data with letters as labels instead of numbers (as long as you don't need more than 26 values).

Pat

messages.subject: Moderated nonlinear factor analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Daniel Bauer
http://dbauer.web.unc.edu/files/2014/08/MET_Bauer_2015-0386R2_Supp.pdf
provides Mplus code to conduct a  moderated nonlinear factor analysis - in  brief, a cfa where in adition to  a direct effect of a  predictor on a manifest indicator of a factor the  factor loading itself can be regressed  on a predictor (or multiple predictor).

I  am wondering if such a  MIMIC model plus a moderated factor loading could  be estimated in lavaan as well (not sure if Lavaan  offers something similar to the  MODEL CONSTRAINT' command)?
Best,
E.

***

Simplified Mplus code for  illustration:

MODEL:

    f1 BY
    y1*
    y2
    y3
    y4(L) ; ! label for the factor  loading, to be used in "MODEL CONSTRAINT"

    f1 ON x1;  ! factor regressed on predictor x1

    y4 ON x1;  ! manifest indicator regressed on predictor x1

MODEL CONSTRAINT:

NEW         (L0 L1);  !  2 new parameter, intercept and slope for regressing the loading  on  !x1

L =   L0 +L1*x1;   ! Moderation of the  factor loading

messages.body_plain:
Dear Pat,

thanks for the reply, and I agree, but I am not sure that this is the issue here. As far as I understand, when declaring variables as ordinal, lavaan does indeed "ignore" the actual values (as they have no meaning like you said) and converts them to an ordered sequence, but then tries to fit an underlying numeric variable. And AFAIK, the values of the latent variables have no intrinsic meaning even for underlying numeric indicators, but group differences should be useful. And what puzzles me here is that when adding measurement equality constraints, the lavPredict-based mean differences increase for the models "assuming" numeric data but decrease for the same models "assuming" ordinal data:

One model for all data:
. numeric (all.n <- cfa (model, data = fdat, estimator = "MLM"): 0.304
. ordinal (all.o <- cfa(model, data = fdat, ordered = T): 0.222

Model with equal indicator intercepts (but not loadings):
. numeric (intcpt.n <- cfa (model, data = fdat, estimator = "MLM", group = "grp", group.equal = "intercepts"): 0.378
. ordinal (intcpt.o <- cfa(model, data = fdat, ordered = T, group = "grp", group.equal = "intercepts"): 0.122
(the estimates from the lavaan summary are 0.385 and 0.284, respectively)

Model with equal indicators and loadings:
. numeric (scal.n <- cfa (model, data = fdat, estimator = "MLM", group = "grp", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts")): 0.442
. ordinal (scal.o <- cfa(model, data = fdat, ordered = T, group = "grp", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts")): 0.108
(the estimates from the lavaan summary are 0.442 and 0.350, respectively)

When constraining the residuals to be equal, too, the predicted factor scores for the MLM model again correspond perfectly to the estimate from the lavaan summary (0.437), for the ordinal model, there is no change compared to the "scal.o" model. Obviously, I am missing something here, especially for the ordinal model.

Best,
Michael

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michael.

Note that your z tests are identical, even though the parameter estimates differ. This indicates a scaling difference. So I suggest looking at the model-implied values of the means and variances of the latents in both models to puzzle this out.

I also didn't notice earlier that you'd run models with invariance of intercepts but not loadings. That's unusual.

Pat

On Sun, Sep 6, 2020 at 2:51 PM Faul R. Sack <derfau...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Pat,
>
> thanks for the reply, and I agree, but I am not sure that this is the issue here. As far as I understand, when declaring variables as ordinal, lavaan does indeed "ignore" the actual values (as they have no meaning like you said) and converts them to an ordered sequence, but then tries to fit an underlying numeric variable. And AFAIK, the values of the latent variables have no intrinsic meaning even for underlying numeric indicators, but group differences should be useful. And what puzzles me here is that when adding measurement equality constraints, the lavPredict-based mean differences increase for the models "assuming" numeric data but decrease for the same models "assuming" ordinal data:
>
> One model for all data:
> . numeric (all.n <- cfa (model, data = fdat, estimator = "MLM"): 0.304
> . ordinal (all.o <- cfa(model, data = fdat, ordered = T): 0.222
>
> Model with equal indicator intercepts (but not loadings):
> . numeric (intcpt.n <- cfa (model, data = fdat, estimator = "MLM", group = "grp", group.equal = "intercepts"): 0.378
> . ordinal (intcpt.o <- cfa(model, data = fdat, ordered = T, group = "grp", group.equal = "intercepts"): 0.122
> (the estimates from the lavaan summary are 0.385 and 0.284, respectively)
>
> Model with equal indicators and loadings:
> . numeric (scal.n <- cfa (model, data = fdat, estimator = "MLM", group = "grp", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts")): 0.442
> . ordinal (scal.o <- cfa(model, data = fdat, ordered = T, group = "grp", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts")): 0.108
> (the estimates from the lavaan summary are 0.442 and 0.350, respectively)
>
> When constraining the residuals to be equal, too, the predicted factor scores for the MLM model again correspond perfectly to the estimate from the lavaan summary (0.437), for the ordinal model, there is no change compared to the "scal.o" model. Obviously, I am missing something here, especially for the ordinal model.
>
> Best,
> Michael
>
> On Sun, Sep 6, 2020 at 3:50 AM Patrick (Malone Quantitative) <mal...@malonequantitative.com> wrote:
> > Michael,
> >
> > That's not something you can expect.
> >
> > When you declare data as ordered, you take away the meaning of the numbers attached to them. A variable with possible values 1, 2, 3, 4 and one with values -93, 0, 5, 10000 are treated the same: four sequential bins. So referring to the "mean" of ordered variables has no meaning.
> >
> > I'm pretty certain, unless instructed otherwise, lavaan treats cfa() factors with ordered indicators as having a latent mean of 0 and variance of 1, regardless of the numeric labels of the indicators, because they really should be treated just as labels. Think of it this way: there's no in-principle reason ordinal methods couldn't be applied to data with letters as labels instead of numbers (as long as you don't need more than 26 values).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Patrick,

thanks again; indeed, I hadn't noticed the identical z values for the scalar invariance model (for the strict invariance and the odd "intercept only equal" model, they differ slightly, BTW), but I don't know (yet) how this could help me out. And you are right about constraining just the intercepts to be equal being "unusual", of course -- this was just to illustrate the opposite tendency of the intercept differences in the numeric vs. ordinal conditions. I would not see this as any kind of useful examination of measurement invariance either.

As mentioned in the first post, the actual issue is an AN(C)OVA-like modeling of group differences with the latent variables as dependents and the same predictor (i.e., group membership; in the actual dataset there are four rather than two groups) having the double role as "measurement invariance criterion" and core predictor of interest. Extracting the latent variable values from the scalar invariance model (preferably for ordinal data, and under the condition of satisfactory model fit, of course) and doing a "conventional" AN(C)OVA seemed like a practical solution to me, but apparently this does not work in a straightforward manner.

Best,
Michael

messages.subject: Re: Moderated nonlinear factor analysis
messages.body_plain:
> I  am wondering if such a  MIMIC model plus a moderated factor loading could  be estimated in lavaan as well

MNLFA is not MIMIC.  In MIMIC, variables are regressed on other variables.  In MNLFA, parameters are regressed on other variables (the latter of which are not even "modeled" variables).  This is a more general case of something like Mplus's TSCORES which allow a different (fixed) Lambda matrix per case in a latent curve model.

lavaan does not allow for this.  The parameters must be considered constant across cases (within each group in a multigroup model).

It is possible in OpenMx.  See work by Dylan Molenaar on heteroskedastic latent trait models, which I think could be considered a special case of MNLFA.  My grad student is working on a tutorial article on MNLFA in OpenMx; I'll try to remember to post a link here once a preprint is available.

> not sure if Lavaan  offers something similar to the  MODEL CONSTRAINT' command)?

Yes, but it only accommodates functions of (estimated) parameters.  Adapted from the ?lavTestWald help page:

HS.model <- '
  visual =~ x1 + b1*x2 + x3
  textual =~ x4 + b2*x5 + x6
  speed =~ x7 + b3*x8 + x9

  ## model constraints
  2*b1 == b3
  b2 - b3 == 0
'
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit)

Variables cannot be used to define constraints, because that would imply parameters vary across cases.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Hi all,

I am trying to fit a moderated mediation model to correspond with the attached diagram, however I am having difficulty including the covariate (child behavior). I know how to include the covariate if I were controlling for it in both a and b paths of the model.

The code I have is below, but I didn't include the covariate (child behavior). Would any be able to suggest how to include it in this formula?

mod_cbcl_i <- "# a path
         att_neg_c ~ 1 + a1 * group

         # b paths
         cbcl_int_t ~ 1 + b1 * att_neg_c
         cbcl_int_t ~ b2 * c_sex
         cbcl_int_t ~ b3 * att_sex

         # c prime path
         cbcl_int_t ~ cp * group

         # index of moderated mediation and conditional indirect effects
         a1b3 := a1 * b3
         maleie := a1 * b1 + a1b3 * 0
         femaleie := a1 * b1 + a1b3 * 1"

I have found several resources online that talk about other moderated mediation models with control variable, but not any for my proposed model. I haven't had a chance to look through all the threads in this forum about moderated mediations, so I apologize if there is an answer already listed here.

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: Moderated Mediation with Covariate
messages.body_plain:
Regardless of what's going on in the rest of the model, the most common way to include a covariate in SEM is to regress all other variables on it.

Note that this might get you in trouble with direction of causality.

Pat

messages.subject: Help with dummy-coded interaction variables in a MIMIC model
messages.subject_clean: Help with dummy-coded interaction variables in a MIMIC model
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm new to SEM and to Lavaan so apologies if this is a straightforward question! My issue is with including (categorical, dummy-coded) interactions as predictors in a SEM model (I’m using Lavaan) and how to interpret the output.

The SEM model I'm trying to build has 3 latent variables as below:
Latent Variable 1: “Latent 1”
Measured by 9 indicator items, scored between 1 (“strongly disagree”) and 5 (“strongly agree”)
Latent Variable 2: “Latent 2”
Measured by 15 indicator items, scored between 1 (“strongly disagree”) and 7 (“strongly agree”)
Latent Variable 3: “Latent 3
Measured by 8 Learner items , scored between 1 (“strongly disagree”) and 7 (“strongly agree”)

It has 5 main predictor variables (all categorical, therefore dummy-coded), as below:
U Type (U1 = 1, U2 = 0)
Country (C1 = 1, C2 = 0)
SES (SESHigh = 1, SESLow = 0)
SSS  (SHigh = 1, SLow = 0)
F Type (F1 = 1, F2 = 0)
And then I want to include interactions between these :
U Type x Country
U Type x F Type
SES x F Type
Country x F Type
SSS x F Type
My issue is how best to include these interactions so that I can interpret the results correctly. As it stands, I have included included only ONE dummy picking up each 2x2 interaction, but then I'm not sure how to interpret the results when that product term is significant. Any help would be really really appreciated!

My code for this is :

library(semTools)
library(lavaan)
library(semPlot)

#data
data = MyData

#define MIMIC
MIMIC6 = '

#Measurement_model
Latent1 =~ A1 + A2 + A3 + A4 + A5 + A6 + A7 + A8 + A9
Latent2=~ C1 + C2 + C3 + C4 + C5 + C6  + C7 + C8 + C9 + C10 + C11 + C12 + C13 + C14 + C15
Latent3 =~  L1 + L2 + L3 + L4 + L5 + L6 + L7 + L8

#Regress DV on group code IVs

Latent1 ~ ~ U1 + C1 + F1 + SESHigh + SHigh + U1xC1 + U1xF1 + SESHighxF1 + C1xF1 + SHighxF1

Consumer ~ U1 + C1 + F1 + SESHigh + SHigh + U1xC1 + U1xF1 + SESHighxF1 + C1xF1 + SHighxF1

Learner ~ ~ U1 + C1 + F1 + SESHigh + SHigh + U1xC1 + U1xF1 + SESHighxF1 + C1xF1 + SHighxF1
'
#run the model
MIMIC6.fit = sem(MIMIC6,
                 missing = "fiml",
                 data = MyData,
                 estimator = "MLR")

#examine the model
summary(MIMIC6.fit,
        standardized = T,
        rsquare = T,
        fit.measures = T)

messages.subject: simple question regarding clustered data
messages.body_plain:
Dear experts,

I am trying to run a moderated mediation analysis with clustered data. I'm new to lavaan and have a simple (I think) question regarding how to include the cluster factor into the model.

I've read a lot about using a multilevel design, but I was wondering if it's also acceptable to just model the moderated mediation on a single level, and then just add the cluster at the end (bolded text below)? My cluster factor comes from the fact that my participants are twins and I need to control for the relatedness between the two individuals within each twin pair.

My current model:
mod1 <- '# a path
         Med ~ 1 + a1 * X
         Med ~ a2 * Mod
         Med ~ a3 * (X * Mod)

         # b path
         Y ~ b1 * Med

         # c prime path
         Y ~ 1 + cp * X

         # index of moderated mediation and conditional indirect effects
         b1a3 := b1 * a3
         Med1ss := a1 + a3 * 1
         Med2ss := a1 + a3 * 2
         Med1 := a1 * b1 + b1a3 * 1
         Med2 := a1 * b1 + b1a3 * 2'

sem.fit1 <- sem(mod1, data = data, cluster = "family")
summary(sem.fit1, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)

Any help would be much appreciated - thank you!

messages.subject: Calculating measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
Dear forum,

I am trying to calculate measurment invariance.
My data includes two groups.

I found the code:
measurementInvariance(model = model_configMI,
                      data = data_both,
                      group = "GP")

Actually, I expected to get the same results as if i test the models against each other by myself. I set up the four models by using the SchroedersGnambs2020 suggestions using reference group (see their Supplement).
However, the metric model (set up by myself) seems to be different to the loadings model (automatically set up in the above code).

These are the results:
Chi-Squared Difference
Test Df AIC BIC Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
fit.configural 1110 37766 39002 2391.0
fit.loadings 1146 37731 38816 2428.4 37.390 36 0.40512
fit.intercepts 1182 37716 38649 2484.9 56.563 36 0.01584 *
fit.means 1182 37716 38649 2484.9 0.000 0

versus
lavTestLRT(fit_config, fit_metric, method="satorra.bentler.2010")

fit_config 1110 37766 39002 2391.0
fit_metric 1146 37857 38941 2554.1 87.808 36 3.22e-06 ***

I wonder which is the better option?
Additionally, my fits are not very good. Considering that the model includes many df the fit is not bad either (and far better than e.g. a single factor model). Is it valid to calculate such difference tests even if the fits are not perfect?

Thanks for any advice,
Stephan

Stephan,

Answering the last point--the likelihood ratio (difference) test only follows the chi-squared distribution if the full model fits perfectly. So while you may accept the full model without good fit (which is an entirely different discussion), you should be aware the p-value for the difference test is going to be incorrect.

Pat

messages.subject: Latent Mean Estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody.
I'm writing here to clarify whether and how Lavaan allows estimating latent variable means. Surfing the WEB (https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/280829/how-to-compute-and-interpret-the-mean-of-a-latent-variable-in-structural-equatio )  I have found this strategy, that proved to be wrong though:

library(lavaan)
data = data("HolzingerSwineford1939")
HS.model =
    "visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
     textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
     speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9

 x1 ~ 0*1 # Setting the intercepts of the manifest variables to zero
 x4 ~ 0*1
 x7 ~ 0*1
 visual ~ 1 # Estimating latent means freely
 textual ~ 1
 speed ~ 1 #

" fit = sem(HS.model,
                  data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
                  meanstructure =TRUE)

Here the user constrains three intercepts of the observed variables to zero (i.e., x1, x4, x7), and then estimate the latent variable intercepts (i.e., visual, textual, and speed). Although the solution seems working, a closer look to the estimated latent variable intercepts (i.e., visual, textual, and speed) reveals that the estimated values are exactly the intercepts for the three indicators now set to zero (i.e., x1, x4, x7), and not the latent mean.

My question is: Is it possible to estimate latent variable means using Lavaan.
If so, which is the correct method?

Thanks in advance

Emanuele

messages.subject: Re: Latent Mean Estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Emanuele.

You actually did estimate latent means, but the way you scaled them gave you answers you didn't expect. Like latent variances, latent means are arbitrary and need to be scaled. The usual way to use latent means is when you have a multiple-group analysis--otherwise, the mean structure is usually unconstrained incidental parameters.

In any case, have you looked at this page of the lavaan tutorial? https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/means.html It shows mean-structures with the H-S data.

What question are you trying to answer with the means?

Pat

messages.subject: Re: Latent Mean Estimation
messages.body_plain:
Emanuele,

No, the loading doesn't have anything to do with it.

The most common method for multiple-group comparisons in my experience is to constrain the intercepts (and loadings) to equality across groups, which puts the latent means on the same metric across groups. Then you set one of the groups to have a latent mean of zero to fix the location. The other group means will be relative to that group.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Emanuele

You can use the measEq.syntax function from semTools to create the syntax from these model for you.
In any case the "actual" mean will be arbitrary and not very meaningful by itself. If you do the meultiple groups apporach the group means will be meaningful in cmparison to each other

## The famous Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6

              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

?measEq.syntax

eq_syn <- measEq.syntax(HS.model, ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",
                          meanstructure=T,
                          group.equal = c("loadings","intercepts"),
                          group="school", data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
cat(as.character( eq_syn ))
summary( eq_syn )

fit <- cfa(as.character( eq_syn ),
           data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
           meanstructure=T, group = "school")
summary(fit)

messages.subject: Re: Moderated Mediation with Covariate
messages.body_plain:
> I was thinking maybe my code would need to look something like this if I was only including the covariate on one path:

If you only regress your mediator on a covariate, I think your indirect effect would be hard to interpret.  The a path would be the effect of group for anyone with the same level of the covariate, but the b paths would not be interpreted as "controlling for the covariate".  In that case, is the indirect effect interpreted as holding the covariate constant or not?  I would follow Pat's advice and use your second syntax.

Of course, you also have sex only predicting the outcome, but it is a moderator, so the b path is a conditional rather than marginal effect.  Preacher et al. (2007) described models with only either a or b moderated, and I don't think there is a contradiction there.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/00273170701341316

messages.subject: Re: Longitudinal CFA with dichotomously scored items
messages.subject_clean: Longitudinal CFA with dichotomously scored items
messages.body_plain:
> 1) Is my code correct for how to treat dichotomously scored items?

Looks fine

> 2) Under the Variances heading in the output, there are Estimates but no Standard Errors. What does that mean?

It means those values are fixed.  In fact, you are using the default parameterization = "delta", so the variances are not even model parameter (well, they are implied by the latent scales, factor loadings, and factor variance).  Here are two informative tutorials, and the Mplus documentation of the parameterizations (which lavaan also uses):

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510701758406

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3162326/

> 3) What does it mean the below warning message disappeared when I added meanstructure=TRUE, std.lv <http://std.lv/>=TRUE?
>

>   lavaan WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!

Not sure why that would only happen when setting the first factor loading to 1.  What does your summary() output look like when you set std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE?  Are the loadings all positive?

It should not be necessary to set meanstructure=TRUE.  That is the default (and necessary) when you have any ordered= outcomes.

> 4) When trying to do longitudinal CFA to test for measurement invariance across time, I got these warning messages:
>
> 1: In lav_samplestats_step2(UNI = FIT, wt = wt, ov.names = ov.names, : lavaan WARNING: correlation between variables X4.T2 and X3.T2 is (nearly) 1.0
>
> 2: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats, : lavaan WARNING: The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (= -8.874240e-4) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified.
>
> It only warns that neighboring items at the same measurement occasion are highly correlated in the longitudinal CFA, not in the individual CFA for that measurement occasion. This makes me wonder if it's due to programming errors on my part.

That doesn't seem plausible, but you can check the estimated polychoric correlations from your longitudinal model and compare them to the estimates from your Time-2 model.

lavInspect(fitT2.CFA, "sampstat")
lavInspect(meq.list[[1]], "sampstat")

> I'm also wondering if warning 2 (non positive-definite variance-covariance matrix) has to do with the large amount of parameters it's estimating with 3 measurement occasions * 14 items each?

Given the size of your model, if your N < 500 or 1000 (depending on the asymmetry of your thresholds), you could expect some instability, and probably a somewhat inflated chi-squared statistic.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.859510

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.882658

> Could this be a numerical integration problem?

lavaan is not using numerical integration.  By default, it uses DWLS estimation.

> Warning 1 was absent in the individual CFA for T2, which makes me wonder if both longitudinal CFA warning messages were a symptom of the same thing

The fact that they appear together makes sense. If 2 variables are so highly correlated, it would make sense that their parameters are probably also have highly correlated sampling distributions, leading to the negative eigenvalue.

> I will be grateful for any advice on what I should be doing differently!

On the help page you reference, I generally advised not to use return.fit=TRUE.  If you are having trouble with estimation, you should be fitting models one at a time so that you know exactly where the problems occur.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Help with dummy-coded interaction variables in a MIMIC model
messages.subject_clean: Help with dummy-coded interaction variables in a MIMIC model
messages.body_plain:
> My issue is how best to include these interactions so that I can interpret the results correctly. As it stands, I have included included only ONE dummy picking up each 2x2 interaction

If you already calculated your product terms as new variables in the data.frame, that is correct.

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

But you could also use the colon operator as a shortcut:

Latent1 ~ U1 + C1 + F1 + SESHigh + SHigh + U1:C1 + U1:F1 + SESHigh:F1 + C1:F1 + SHigh:F1

FYI, you have an extra tilde after Latent1 and Learner.

> then I'm not sure how to interpret the results when that product term is significant.

Probe the interaction.

http://quantpsy.org/interact/interactions.htm

You can label the paths and calculate user-defined parameters that represent the conditional effects you want to test.  For example, if U1:C1 is significant, and you want to probe the effect of U1 for each level of C1:

Latent1 ~ b_u1*U1 + b_c1*C1 + F1 + SESHigh + SHigh + b_int*U1xC1 + ...

## user-defined parameters to probe interaction
# b_u1 is already the effect of U1 when C1 == 0 (and F1 == 0)
b_u1_c1 := b_u1 + b_int # effect of U1 when C1 == 1 (and F1 == 0)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Latent interaction problems (indProd,SEM,probe2WayMC)
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,
I'm trying to model a latent interaction in a SEM using the WLSMV due to categorical indicators on my outcome variables (I & E). The interaction is between age (observed variable) and three latent constructs. Therefore, I'm using the indProd-package to calculate the respective product-terms.
The model terminates normally without any error. When I try to probe my interaction using the probe2WayMC function, I'm getting the following error:

Error in est$beta[nameY,nameX]: subscript out of bounds.

This is my syntax:

dat<- indProd(dat,
              c("age"),
              c("NoSKMSM" , "KSMChrMX" , "KSMSMx",
                "NoSN"  , "NChrMX" , "NSMx",
                "NoSEMnew", "EMChrMX"  , "EMSMX"),
              residualC=T,
              match=F,
              names=c("age_anos","age_achr","age_as",
                      "age_nnos","age_nchr","age_ns",
                      "age_enos","age_echr","age_es"))

mod <- '

#Latente Faktoren

                 A   =~ NoSKMSM  + KSMChrMX + KSMSMx
                 N   =~ NoSN   + NChrMX + NSMx
                 EM  =~ NoSEMnew + EMChrMX  + EMSMX
                 I   =~ D_VORH + A_VORH + AIMAX
                 E   =~ O_VORH + C_VORH  + AD_MAX

#Latente Ieraktionen

                 Mod_A_age =~ age_anos + age_as + age_achr
                 Mod_N_age =~ age_nnos + age_ns + age_nchr
                 Mod_em_age =~ age_enos + age_es + age_echr

                 Mod_A_age ~  0*age
                 Mod_A_age ~~ 0*A
                 Mod_N_age ~  0*age
                 Mod_N_age ~~ 0*N
                 Mod_em_age ~  0*age
                 Mod_em_age ~~ 0*EM

################################################## Regressionen

                 I ~ A + N + EM + age + sex +  Mod_A_age + Mod_N_age + Mod_em_age
                 E ~ A + N + EM + age + sex +  Mod_A_age + Mod_N_age + Mod_em_age

################################################## latente Korrelationen

                 A ~~ EM + N
                 # A ~ KB
                 N ~~ EM
                 # N ~ KB
                 # EM  ~ KB
                 I ~~ E
                  '

sem2_mod <- sem(mod,
                data=dat,
                estimator = "WLSMV",
                mimic="Mplus",
                start="Mplus",
                meanstructure = T,
                ordered = c("D_VORH",
                            "A_VORH",
                            "AIMAX",
                            "O_VORH",
                            "C_VORH",
                            "AD_MAX"))

summary(sem2_mod,
        fit.measures = TRUE,
        standardize  = TRUE,
        rsquare      = TRUE,
        estimates    = TRUE,
        ci           = FALSE)

probe2WayMC(sem2_mod,
            nameX = c("age", "A" , "N" , "EM" ,"sex","KB", "Mod_A_age", "Mod_N_age",
            "Mod_em_age"),
            nameY = "I",
            modVar = "age",
            valProbe= c(4,16))

Any hints on how to solve the problem are highly appreciated. I'm also not sure if I should use the probe2WayMC or RC-function. I'm guessing, if I select ResidualC=T in the indProd-function, RC would be appropriate. However, that gives me a similar error regarding the est$psi.
Thanks in advance!

messages.subject: Re: full information maximum Likelihood
messages.body_plain:
On 9/13/20 2:53 PM, Guido wrote:
> Yves, no I am not looking for the missing= ml option. My data is
> complete and I want to make sure it uses the item responses as input and
> not te correlation matrix of the dataframe.

If you use ML, and the data is complete, then lavaan will use the sample
covariance matrix of your data.frame. However, if one would use casewise
estimation instead (using the raw data), the results would be identical.

> And if I use another
> estimator like DWLS? It is still full information?

No. DWLS is a limited-information estimator. Only useful for categorical
data.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: A problem with the nonlinear model
messages.body_plain:
You can't use (eg) 'X11*X82' for a product term. In lavaan syntax, 'X11'
is used as a label.

The best approach here is to first create all those product terms (and
call them eg X11.X82) and add them to your data.frame. Then, you can use
them as any other variable.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
I meant content-wise.

If your variables are best treated as ordered, then multiplying them doesn't make sense. For example, VarA =2 and VarB = 2 gives VarAB = 4. But so does VarA = 1 and VarB =4.  This is fine if VarA and VarB are interval, and the difference between 1 and 2 is half the difference between 2 and 4. But if you can't make that assumption, then having VarAB come out the same for the two situations may not be reasonable.

So the question is whether the gain in being able to use product terms is worth the cost of forcing ordinal variables into an interval-variable framework. That's why I asked what the variables represent, so you can think about whether that cost is worth paying in your particular situation.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: Error message in measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
> I am trying to evaluate partial metric invariance using the "measurementInvariance" argument.

The measurementInvariance() function is only designed to evaluate different levels of full invariance (i.e., all loadings, all intercepts, etc.).  There is a partialInvariance() function that provides post hoc tests for individual items.

> Error in measurementInvariance(model = my_model, data = my_data, group.partial = "sex")

There is no group.partial= argument to the measurementInvariance() function.  It can be passed to lavaan(), but see the ?lavOptions help page for the description of how to actually use it (it accepts parameters, not the name of a grouping variable).  I think you mean to set group="sex", which would resolve the error of having only 1 group (because you did not correctly provide a grouping variable).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Latent interaction problems (indProd,SEM,probe2WayMC)
messages.body_plain:
> I'm trying to model a latent interaction in a SEM using the WLSMV due to categorical indicators on my outcome variables (I & E). The interaction is between age (observed variable) and three latent constructs. Therefore, I'm using the indProd-package to calculate the respective product-terms.

Product indicators are only appropriate for continuous indicators.  There is not a "product" of 2 categories.

Here is a recent paper that compared some methods for categorical indicators.

https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0013164419865017

With only 3 indicators per factor, their recommended parceling strategy is not an option.  If you have at least 5 categories, I expect you could get away with simply treating the items as continuous, in which case you could use product indicators as you intended.

> I'm also not sure if I should use the probe2WayMC or RC-function. I'm guessing, if I select ResidualC=T in the indProd-function, RC would be appropriate.

Correct.

> Error in est$beta[nameY,nameX]: subscript out of bounds.

I expect the problem is that the function expects the first-order effects to be latent variable names as well.  You have interactions of latent variables with age, which is observed.  I would recommend treating it like a single-indicator construct (which is what lavaan does internally without telling you, to save you the trouble):

AGE =~ age
age ~~ 0*age

Then use AGE in the rest of your syntax in place of age.

But also make sure you are using the latest development version of the package, just in case this was an old bug that was already resolved.  In a fresh R session, run:

devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

Then restart R before running your script.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Longitudinal CFA with dichotomously scored items
messages.body_plain:
> How high is too high?

I'd say they both are, but clearly lavaan only issues the message when the polychoric correlation is closer to 1 than 0.96

>
> I’m considering item parceling but am unsure of the implications of doing that at just one measurement occasion when testing for longitudinal measurement invariance.

 If you do it, you should do it at all occasions.  Alternatively, you could simply choose one or the other as an indicator, discarding the other (again, at all occasions), but I would only do that if the two items were nearly identical at all occasions.  You can check 2-way contingency tables for that pair at each occasion to see how (non)redundant the variables are.

table(data$X4.T1, data$X3.T1)
table(data$X4.T2, data$X3.T2)
table(data$X4.T3, data$X3.T3)

>  3) With no missing data treatment, the sample size is under 300 at each measurement occasion and is 117 for the longitudinal CFA.

That is why your polychorics differ between the full and T-2 models.  They are being fit to different data.

>
> Is this too small for a model with 3 measurement occasions and 14 items per measurement occasion?

Certainly yes.  You are estimating 129 parameters in the full configural model, which is > N.  Even if you set missing="pairwise", you would have very few observations per estimated parameter. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2012.04.010

messages.subject: Re: full information maximum Likelihood
messages.body_plain:
> I want to make sure it uses the item responses as input

You mean like Mplus offers?  That is marginal ML estimation, and you can request it in lavaan with estimator = "MML"

HS9 <- HolzingerSwineford1939[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5",
                                 "x6","x7","x8","x9")]
HSbinary <- as.data.frame( lapply(HS9, cut, 2, labels=FALSE) )
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HSbinary, ordered=names(HSbinary), estimator = "MML")

But it is an experimental feature, and you will see that it runs veeeeeery sloooooowly (numerical integration) and might not even converge for models with more than 1 or 2 constructs (dimensions across which to integrate).

If you want a ML estimator for ordinal data, consider the much more efficient pairwise ML estimator, estimator = "PML"

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2012.04.010

But as the name suggests, it is still limited information. But each pairwise likelihood is calculated using full information available for that pair of variables.  Read the paper for details.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> --> Now, I get this error message: " lavaan ERROR: some latent variable names collide with observed variable names: PBI" and I don't know what it means or what I should do.

Try searching for a solution in the group first.  Entering that error message into the search bar at the top of the lavaan group returned this result (right below your own post):

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/jVujbaDAsbc/Kdin7P2JCAAJ

> It says that the measurementInvariance function is deprecated

You can still use deprecated functions, they just won't be around forever.  I won't remove it for a few more years, after I build a replacement that doesn't require separate functions for continuous/categorical or group/longitudinal invariance, and does not proceed to fit more restrictive models even when less restrictive hypotheses can already be rejected.  In the meantime, I recommend transitioning to measEq.syntax() only because it is already more general, and has a pedagogical orientation if you use it as directed (i.e., to generate lavaan syntax, which you can then check to verify and perhaps learn from).

In your case, this is how you could generate syntax for the configural and metric invariance models (adapting the help-page examples to your own model/data).

# configural invariance
stx.config <- measEq.syntax(cfa_SOgirls, data = data.female,
                            ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv/>", group = "Country_Code")
summary(stx.config) # verify the features of this model/data
mod.config <- as.character(stx.config) # save as a character string
fit.config <- cfa(mod.config, data = data.female, missing = "fiml") # fit model

# metric invariance
stx.metric <- measEq.syntax(cfa_SOgirls, data = data.female,
                            ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv/>", group = "Country_Code",
                            group.equal = "loadings")
summary(stx.metric) # verify the features of this model/data
mod.metric <- as.character(stx.metric) # save as a character string
fit.metric <- cfa(mod.metric, data = data.female, missing = "fiml") # fit model

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence,

thanks a lot for the helpful suggestions!
I guess I did not point out one important detail: My indicators are continuous, my outcome variables are not. Thus, I thought the product-indicator approach should work.

The advise you gave regarding the age-variable seems to be working. Additionally, I did play around a bit and realized, that the probe2WayMC-function works by only entering the variables that are part of the interaction. Thus, I threw out all the other independent variables and probed each interaction individually. I would be very happy for another hint if that approach is not feasible in your eyes.

Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Montag, 14. September 2020 um 15:17:34 UTC+2:
> > I'm trying to model a latent interaction in a SEM using the WLSMV due to categorical indicators on my outcome variables (I & E). The interaction is between age (observed variable) and three latent constructs. Therefore, I'm using the indProd-package to calculate the respective product-terms.
>
> Product indicators are only appropriate for continuous indicators.  There is not a "product" of 2 categories.
>
> Here is a recent paper that compared some methods for categorical indicators.
>
> https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0013164419865017
>
> With only 3 indicators per factor, their recommended parceling strategy is not an option.  If you have at least 5 categories, I expect you could get away with simply treating the items as continuous, in which case you could use product indicators as you intended.
>
> > I'm also not sure if I should use the probe2WayMC or RC-function. I'm guessing, if I select ResidualC=T in the indProd-function, RC would be appropriate.
>
> Correct.
>
> > Error in est$beta[nameY,nameX]: subscript out of bounds.
>
> I expect the problem is that the function expects the first-order effects to be latent variable names as well.  You have interactions of latent variables with age, which is observed.  I would recommend treating it like a single-indicator construct (which is what lavaan does internally without telling you, to save you the trouble):
>
> AGE =~ age
> age ~~ 0*age
>
> Then use AGE in the rest of your syntax in place of age.
>
> But also make sure you are using the latest development version of the package, just in case this was an old bug that was already resolved.  In a fresh R session, run:
>
> devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")
>
> Then restart R before running your script.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.body_plain:
> How can I reduce the high correlations between them to solve the problem

Did you use the semTools::indProd() function to calculate product indicators?  Read the References listed on the help page; I think the residualizing option implies the nonlinear-term factors would be orthogonal to the lower-order factors, but I don't remember.  Orthogonality might also require estimating residual covariances among product indicators which shared the same lower-order indicator (I forget all the details of that approach, I read that article back in 2011).  I usually recommend the default (double-mean-centering) approach, but you have quadratic as well as interaction terms in your model, so it's pretty complex.  Consider also looking into the LMS estimation available in the nlsem  <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nlsem/>package <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nlsem/>.

FYI, this is a warning, not an error.  Your model ran, and there is nothing surprising about multicollinearity among terms when some predictors are functions of other predictors.  If your nonlinear effects are not significant, you can remove them from the model to make it simpler, which would reduce the amount of multicollinearity simply by having fewer nonlinear terms.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: avaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite;
messages.body_plain:
To add to what Terrence said. With residual centering (orthogonalizing) the latent interaction/non-linear factors are uncorrelated with any lower order terms (and I believe they should be uncorrelated with each other, but that depends on how things were residual centered). With double mean centering the latent interactions/non-linear terms should be allowed to covary with lower order terms and each other too. Based on the results above, I'd be really surprised if either of those approaches were used (and the first thing I'd do is take a look at the indProd function and use one of those two approaches. For complex models (at least models with 3-way interactions there's some evidence that residual centering provides less bias than double mean centering: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0013164412445473 but that is under a case where assumptions for residual centering are met)

In terms of including residual covariances among the indicators, that depends on if you're using a matched pair strategy to create indicators or if you're creating all possible pairs of indicators. If you use a matched pair strategy, then there's no need for residual covariances, since there's no overlap among indicators of the latent interaction/non-linear variable, if you use all possible pairs of indicators then you need to include residual covariances (this is true whether you use double mean centering or residual centering).

Alex

messages.body_plain:
Callum,

Your sem() call to create mediation_model_fit is for data=LMRS. Your factors are latent and are not part of the LMRS dataset, so sem() can't find them. You need to define the factors in the same model as you specify the structural (i.e., '~') relations.

Pat

> To add to what Terrence said. With residual centering (orthogonalizing) the latent interaction/non-linear factors are uncorrelated with any lower order terms (and I believe they should be uncorrelated with each other, but that depends on how things were residual centered). With double mean centering the latent interactions/non-linear terms should be allowed to covary with lower order terms and each other too. Based on the results above, I'd be really surprised if either of those approaches were used (and the first thing I'd do is take a look at the indProd function and use one of those two approaches. For complex models (at least models with 3-way interactions there's some evidence that residual centering provides less bias than double mean centering: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0013164412445473 but that is under a case where assumptions for residual centering are met)
>
> In terms of including residual covariances among the indicators, that depends on if you're using a matched pair strategy to create indicators or if you're creating all possible pairs of indicators. If you use a matched pair strategy, then there's no need for residual covariances, since there's no overlap among indicators of the latent interaction/non-linear variable, if you use all possible pairs of indicators then you need to include residual covariances (this is true whether you use double mean centering or residual centering).
>
> Alex
>
> On Tuesday, September 15, 2020 at 5:43:59 AM UTC-4 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > > How can I reduce the high correlations between them to solve the problem
> >
> > Did you use the semTools::indProd() function to calculate product indicators?  Read the References listed on the help page; I think the residualizing option implies the nonlinear-term factors would be orthogonal to the lower-order factors, but I don't remember.  Orthogonality might also require estimating residual covariances among product indicators which shared the same lower-order indicator (I forget all the details of that approach, I read that article back in 2011).  I usually recommend the default (double-mean-centering) approach, but you have quadratic as well as interaction terms in your model, so it's pretty complex.  Consider also looking into the LMS estimation available in the nlsem  <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nlsem/>package <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nlsem/>.
> >
> > FYI, this is a warning, not an error.  Your model ran, and there is nothing surprising about multicollinearity among terms when some predictors are functions of other predictors.  If your nonlinear effects are not significant, you can remove them from the model to make it simpler, which would reduce the amount of multicollinearity simply by having fewer nonlinear terms.

messages.subject: Re: Can I mix categorical and continuous variables in SEM ?
messages.subject_clean: Can I mix categorical and continuous variables in SEM ?
messages.body_plain:
> Can I mix categorical and continuous variables in SEM?

Yes.

> can I use question C alone instead of using latent variable f2 (estimated by C&D)?

Yes, you can treat f2 as a single-indicator construct (i.e., leave D out of your model), but do that at all time points if you want to interpret your autoregressive paths or compare cross-lagged parameters over time.  Make sure f1 has loading-invariance constraints in place over time as well (although it is not really testable with so few indicators).

messages.subject: InformativeTesting with 'control' variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am have a specific issue with the InformativeTesting function when testing order constraints in a LGC model with an exogenous ‘control’ variable.

I am helping write a pre-registration where the authors plan to fit a LGC model with an exogenous continuous control variable (household income) and a categorical grouping variable (perceived relative income inequality; PRIE). They want to test whether a certain category of the categorical grouping variable (those who perceive themselves as poorer) does ‘worse’ than the other categories, which is why I am fitting a LGC model with order constraints.

I simulated some data where the order constraints are clearly true/present, however I am having trouble with the InformativeTesting function. In short, the InformativeTesting function successfully identifies the order constraints being present in the data when I do not include the exogenous ‘control’ variable in the model (Type A test p < 0.05; Type B test p > 0.05); however, once I include the exogenous ‘control' variable in the model the function produces a result that there are not order constraints present (Type A test p > 0.05; Type B test p > 0.05). This even occurs if I simulate the data in such a way that there is no correlation between the exogenous ‘control’ variable and the categorical variable which is used for the order constraints.

As there are no examples online of the InformativeTesting function used with control variables in the model, I am unsure whether the issue I am experiencing is because the function is not designed to be used on such models?

I have added a toy example below. Any help/pointers would be greatly appreciated.

Best wishes,
Amy

## Toy example of Informative.Testing issue
### Orben, Amy; 16.09.2020
## This is an example to show how the informative.testing function ceases to pick up a order constraint in simulated data
## when an exogenous 'control' variable is added.
## For a pre-registration I am hoping to test for order constraints in a model with multiple 'control' variables
## so I need to address this issue. Further, if there is a way to constrain the parameters of the 'control' variables
## (e.g. income in this toy example) to be equal for the categorical variable used to test the order constraints
## I would love to know!

library(lavaan)
library(tidyverse)

# Simulate data

## simulate LCS model data with two exogenous variables (income and perceived relative income inequality)
set.seed(1234)
simulate_model <-'
x_2 ~ 1*x_1
dx =~ 1*x_2
x_2 ~ 0*1
x_2 ~~ 0*x_2

dx ~ -1*1        # This fixes the intercept of the change score
x_1 ~ 10*1       # This fixes the intercept of x_1

dx ~~ 2*dx    # This fixes the variance of the change score
x_1 ~~ 3*x_1  # This fixes the variance of the x_1

dx~0*x_1   # This fixes the self-feedback parameter to 0.

###### We now add the two exogenous variables
### household income (income) and perceived relative income inequality (prie)
x_1 ~ 0.05*income
dx ~ 0*income
income ~~ 0.2*income
income ~ 5.9*1

x_1 ~ -0.4*prie
dx ~ -0.9*prie
prie ~~ 0.3*prie
prie ~ 1.5*1

prie ~~ -0.2*income
'

## Simulate data
simdat<-simulateData(simulate_model, sample.nobs = 1000, meanstructure = T)

## Make PRIE into a categorical variables with three levels
simdat$prie <- cut_number(simdat$prie, 3, labels = c("rich", "same", "poor"))

# Order Constraints Testing
## We create two models, one without the exogenous control variable and one with the exogenous control variables

## Create model without exogenous 'control' variable (income)
model_withoutincome <- '
x_2 ~ 1*x_1
dx =~ 1*x_2
x_2 ~ 0*1
x_2 ~~ 0*x_2

dx ~ c(c_p,c_s,c_r)*1
x_1 ~ c(i_p,i_s,i_r)*1
dx ~~ dx
x_1 ~~ x_1
dx ~ x_1
'

## create model with exogenous 'control' variable (income)
model_withincome <- '
x_2 ~ 1*x_1
dx =~ 1*x_2
x_2 ~ 0*1
x_2 ~~ 0*x_2

dx ~ c(c_p,c_s,c_r)*1
x_1 ~ c(i_p,i_s,i_r)*1
dx ~~ dx
x_1 ~~ x_1
dx ~ x_1

dx ~ income
x_1 ~ income
income ~~ income
income ~ 1
'

## specify constraints
constraints <- '
c_p < c_r
c_p < c_s

i_p < i_r
i_p < i_s
'

## run informative testing on both models
test_withoutincome <- InformativeTesting(model = model_withoutincome, data = simdat,
                                               constraints = constraints,
                                               double.bootstrap = "no",
                                               R = 10, group = "prie",
                                               parallel = "multicore", ncpus = 8)
test_withincome <- InformativeTesting(model = model_withincome, data = simdat,
                                            constraints = constraints,
                                            double.bootstrap = "no",
                                            R = 10, group = "prie",
                                            parallel = "multicore", ncpus = 8)
# Results

## the model that does not include the exogenous control variable succeeds in picking up the simulated order constraints
test_withoutincome

## the model that includes the exogenous control variable however fails in doing so
test_withincome

## Note: the problem persists if I simulate data without a correlation between income and prie

messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much - that worked! I didn't know you could simulate multiple groups in the simulateData function, so I am glad I learnt this today.

I copied the working code below for those interested.

## Toy example of Informative.Testing issue
### Orben, Amy; 16.09.2020
## This is an example to show how the informative.testing function ceases to pick up a order constraint in simulated data
## when an exogenous 'control' variable is added.
## For a pre-registration I am hoping to test for order constraints in a model with multiple 'control' variables
## so I need to address this issue. Further, if there is a way to constrain the parameters of the 'control' variables
## (e.g. income in this toy example) to be equal for the categorical variable used to test the order constraints
## I would love to know!

# Simulate data
library(lavaan)
library(tidyverse)

## simulate LCS model data with two exogenous variables (income and perceived relative income inequality)
set.seed(1234)
simulate_model <-'
x_2 ~ 1*x_1
dx =~ 1*x_2
x_2 ~ 0*1
x_2 ~~ 0*x_2

dx ~ c(-1.5,-1.2,-1)*1        # This fixes the intercept of the change score
x_1 ~ c(8,10,12)*1       # This fixes the intercept of x_1

dx ~~ 2*dx    # This fixes the variance of the change score
x_1 ~~ 3*x_1  # This fixes the variance of the x_1

dx~0*x_1   # This fixes the self-feedback parameter to 0.

###### We now add the two exogenous variables
### household income (income) and perceived relative income inequality (prie)
x_1 ~ 0.05*income
dx ~ 0*income
income ~~ 0.2*income

income ~ c(4.5,5.9,6.1)*1
'

## Simulate data
simdat<-simulateData(simulate_model, sample.nobs = c(3300,3300,3300), meanstructure = T, group.label=c('poor','same','rich'))
simdat$group <- dplyr::recode(simdat$group, `1` = "poor", `2` = "same", `3` = "rich")

# Order Constraints Testing
## We create two models, one without the exogenous control variable and one with the exogenous control variables

## Create model without exogenous 'control' variable (income)
model_withoutincome <- '
x_2 ~ 1*x_1
dx =~ 1*x_2
x_2 ~ 0*1
x_2 ~~ 0*x_2

dx ~ c(c_p,c_s,c_r)*1
x_1 ~ c(i_p,i_s,i_r)*1
dx ~~ dx
x_1 ~~ x_1
dx ~ x_1
'

## create model with exogenous 'control' variable (income)
model_withincome <- '
x_2 ~ 1*x_1
dx =~ 1*x_2
x_2 ~ 0*1
x_2 ~~ 0*x_2

dx ~ c(c_p,c_s,c_r)*1
x_1 ~ c(i_p,i_s,i_r)*1
dx ~~ dx
x_1 ~~ x_1
dx ~ x_1

dx ~ income
x_1 ~ income
income ~~ income
income ~ 1
'

## specify constraints
constraints <- '
c_p < c_r
c_p < c_s

i_p < i_r
i_p < i_s
'

## run informative testing on both models
test_withoutincome <- InformativeTesting(model = model_withoutincome, data = simdat,
                                               constraints = constraints,
                                               double.bootstrap = "no",

                                               R = 10, group = "group",

                                               parallel = "multicore", ncpus = 8)
test_withincome <- InformativeTesting(model = model_withincome, data = simdat,
                                            constraints = constraints,
                                            double.bootstrap = "no",

                                            R = 10, group = "group",

                                            parallel = "multicore", ncpus = 8)
# Results

## the model that does not include the exogenous control variable succeeds in picking up the simulated order constraints
test_withoutincome

## the model that includes the exogenous control variable however fails in doing so
test_withincome

messages.subject: Re: understanding robust CFI and TLI statistics when using WLSMV
messages.subject_clean: understanding robust CFI and TLI statistics when using WLSMV
messages.body_plain:
> the CFI and TLI had .861 and .848 as values, respectively, in the second column of the output, which I interpret these to mean that they are robust values

They are calculated using the scaled (robust) chi-squared values in that column, but they only use the original formulas for CFI/TLI/RMSEA that were not designed for robust statistics.

The ones explicitly labeled "robust CFI" etc. have modified formulas for robust statistics.  This article illuminates differences, and cites their origins.

https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2018.1455142

> with fitMeasures(), I saw that these values were labeled under "cfi.scaled" and "tli.scaled" whereas "cfi.robust" and "tli.robust" had "NAs" as values.

The ones labeled scaled simply use the scaled chi-squared in original formulas.  The ones explicitly labeled robust use the modified formulas for robust statistics.

Searching for this topic in the group's search bar should have returned several past threads on the same topic.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: How can I construct single-indicator latent variable model?
messages.body_plain:
Hello community members,

● What I actually want to do
- I'm trying to analyze panel data with lavaan package (cross-lagged effect model).
- If I could I wanted to run following code

model <- '
# Observed variables A,B,C,D are ordinal variables
f1 =~ 1*A1 + B1;
f2 =~ 1*A2 + B2;
f3 =~ 1*C1 + D1;
f4 =~ 1*C2 + D2;

f3 ~ f1 + f2;
f4 ~ f1 + f2
'
result <- sem(model, data, ordered = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

● Problem
- But I actually don't have D1 (in 3rd line in the former model).

● My code
- So I changed my model to one containing single-indicator latent variable.
- As follows, I fix the coefficient of the C1 at one and error variance of it

f1 =~ 1*A1 + B1;
f2 =~ 1*A2 + B2;
f3 =~ 1*C1;
f4 =~ 1*C2 + D2;

#Raw Cronbach's alpha is 0.783 and var is 0.957
C1 ~~ (1-0.783)*0.957*C1

f3 ~ f1 + f2;
f4 ~ f1 + f2
'
result <- sem(model, data, ordered = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

But I still have these warning messages.

lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
lavaan WARNING: could not invert information matrix needed for robust test statistic

- How can I solve this problem and identify the models?

I thank you in advance.

messages.body_plain:

Thank you so much for the article,  your helpful response, and patience.  And I am sorry (and very embarrassed) for not having searched before asking the same question.

Thank you again and have a wonderful day!

Anh

On Thursday, September 17, 2020 at 5:29:00 AM UTC-4 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > the CFI and TLI had .861 and .848 as values, respectively, in the second column of the output, which I interpret these to mean that they are robust values
>
> They are calculated using the scaled (robust) chi-squared values in that column, but they only use the original formulas for CFI/TLI/RMSEA that were not designed for robust statistics.
>
> The ones explicitly labeled "robust CFI" etc. have modified formulas for robust statistics.  This article illuminates differences, and cites their origins.
>
> https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2018.1455142
>
> > with fitMeasures(), I saw that these values were labeled under "cfi.scaled" and "tli.scaled" whereas "cfi.robust" and "tli.robust" had "NAs" as values.
>
> The ones labeled scaled simply use the scaled chi-squared in original formulas.  The ones explicitly labeled robust use the modified formulas for robust statistics.
>
> Searching for this topic in the group's search bar should have returned several past threads on the same topic.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: SEM - multigroup
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I'm new to this group, so sorry if I may not comply with the group-netiquette.

I'm working with SEM in social-mobility framework as I want to use different survey-questions to define the cognitive ability as a latent factor and in turn use it as an exogenous regression path.
The model is defined as follows:

sem<- '
#Measurement model - latent variables
ability =~ c_cgwri_dv + c_cgwrd_dv + c_cgs7ca_dv + c_cgvfc_dv + c_cgna_dv
education=~edu_r
r_class=~respondent_class
o_class=~max_class
agree =~ c_big5a_dv
consc =~ c_big5c_dv
neur =~ c_big5n_dv
open =~ c_big5o_dv
extro =~ c_big5e_dv

#Structural model - Pahts
ability ~ a*o_class
education ~ b*ability + c*o_class + d*agree + e*consc + f*neur + g*open + h*extro
r_class ~ i*education + l*ability + m*o_class + n*agree + o*consc + p*neur + q*open + r*extro

#Indirect effects:
i_ability := b*i
i_originclass := (a*l) + (c*i) + (a*b*i)
i_agree := d*i
i_consc := e*i
i_neur := f*i
i_open := g*i
i_extro := h*i

#Correlations
c_cgwri_dv ~~ c_cgwrd_dv
c_cgs7ca_dv ~~ c_cgna_dv
c_cgwri_dv ~~ c_cgvfc_dv
c_cgwrd_dv ~~ c_cgvfc_dv
c_cgvfc_dv ~~ c_cgna_dv
c_cgs7ca_dv ~~ c_cgvfc_dv
agree ~~ ability
consc ~~ ability
neur ~~ ability
open ~~ ability
extro ~~ ability
o_class ~~ agree + consc + neur + open + extro
'

I want to perform a multi-group analysis by gender and therefore I was comparing the free and constrained model to check for differences. messages.subject_clean: CFA warning not identified but df > 0
messages.body_plain:
Vibeke,

Negative correlations and covariances are not a concern, just variances. For a trivial example, income and homelessness would be negatively correlated.

The identification problem for the first message was, as you're starting to see, that you had only two indicators for comp4. In a CFA, each factor needs at least three indicators in the absence of additional constraints to be identified.

Non-negative degrees of freedom is necessary for identification of the full model, but not sufficient, because parts of a model can be locally unidentified, as was your case with comp4.

Pat

Hello,

I've seen a few posts about this, but I haven't seen any clear answers and I am wondering if there have been any updates on this. I am trying to run (what seems like) a simple multilevel SEM and I keep getting an error that I do not understand. Here's the basic structure of my model:

mlsem <-'
level: 1
    XW =~ X1 + X2 + X3
    MW =~ M1 + M2 + M3
    YW =~ Y1 + Y2 + Y3
    MW ~ XW
    YW ~ MW + XW
level: 2

    XB =~ X1 + X2 + X3
    MB =~ M1 + M2 + M3
    YB =~ Y1 + Y2 + Y3
    MB ~ XB
    YB ~ MB + XB
'

When I try to run
    fit2<- sem(mlsem, data=data, cluster="ï..ID")
    summary(fit1, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=T,rsquare=T)
I get an error that says "Error in if (fx.delta < tol) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed"

What does this mean? Does my model seem to be okay, or is there something wrong in my model specification that is producing this error?

Any advice would be so appreciated! Please let me know if I can provide any additional info.

--------------------------------
Allycen R. Kurup, B.S.

Clinical Psychology Graduate Student
Purdue University

messages.subject: Problems with reproducing results for a measurement invariance test
messages.subject_clean: Problems with reproducing results for a measurement invariance test
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am currently working on examining longitudinal measurement invariance in a 9-wave
annual dataset for a 3-item measure of self-esteem. In one analysis, I wrote
the script (model_1), shown below, using the cfa() function. I fit this to a
wide version of my dataset (i.e., one row per participant with the assessments
per wave as different variables). I found that the model fit for the configural
model was CFI = .849, RMSEA = .059, and very similarly for the weak model, CFI
= .849, RMSEA = .059.

However, I found a technical paper in which invariance was tested for the same
dataset using the now-deprecated measurementInvariance() function (model_2),
shown below. In this paper, a long version of the dataset was used (i.e., one
row per assessment wave). They reported different fit statistics, so that for
the configural model, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000, and for the weak model, CFI =
.995, RMSEA = .054.

To better understand where the difference in fit came from, I inspected the
code behind the measurementInvariance() function, which I then tested in the
long dataset with the cfa() subcommand “group=“wave” (model_3), shown below. This
model yielded the same fit statistics as the model I fit with the measurementInvariance()
command. I then tried to write out the model fully in longhand (i.e., without
using the “group =” subcommand in the cfa() function; see model_4). However, if
I fit this model to the wide dataset I am unable to replicate the statistics of
model 2 and 3, and instead get a model fit of CFI = .616, RMSEA = .105.

My question now is why model 4 does not yield the same estimates as models 2
and 3 do. Is there a mistake in my model specification? Or is there a logical
reason for why the estimates differ that I’m missing?

Many thanks in advance for your help.

Best,
Elisabeth de Moor

model_1 <- ' SE_02 =~ NA*per1i2.2 +
lambda1*per1i2.2 + per1i7.2 + per1i13.2
                SE_03 =~ NA*per1i2.3 +

                SE_07 =~ NA*per1i2.7 +
lambda1*per1i2.7 + per1i7.7 + per1i13.7
                SE_08 =~ NA*per1i2.8 +
lambda1*per1i2.8 + per1i7.8 + per1i13.8
                SE_09 =~ NA*per1i2.9 +
