On Tue, Sep 22, 2020, 3:48 PM Elisabeth de Moor <e.l.d...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear all,
>
> I am currently working on examining longitudinal measurement invariance in a 9-wave annual dataset for a 3-item measure of self-esteem. In one analysis, I wrote the script (model_1), shown below, using the cfa() function. I fit this to a wide version of my dataset (i.e., one row per participant with the assessments per wave as different variables). I found that the model fit for the configural model was CFI = .849, RMSEA = .059, and very similarly for the weak model, CFI = .849, RMSEA = .059.
>
> However, I found a technical paper in which invariance was tested for the same dataset using the now-deprecated measurementInvariance() function (model_2), shown below. In this paper, a long version of the dataset was used (i.e., one row per assessment wave). They reported different fit statistics, so that for the configural model, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000, and for the weak model, CFI = .995, RMSEA = .054.
>
> To better understand where the difference in fit came from, I inspected the code behind the measurementInvariance() function, which I then tested in the long dataset with the cfa() subcommand “group=“wave” (model_3), shown below. This model yielded the same fit statistics as the model I fit with the measurementInvariance() command. I then tried to write out the model fully in longhand (i.e., without using the “group =” subcommand in the cfa() function; see model_4). However, if I fit this model to the wide dataset I am unable to replicate the statistics of model 2 and 3, and instead get a model fit of CFI = .616, RMSEA = .105.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terence,

 thanks for providing the measurement invariance functions! I have a question regarding partial invariance.

 I want to examine the measurement invariance of a construct called "Demands". At both measurement points the construct was measured with three items each.

 I have calculated a model for the configural invariance and a model for the metric invariance. The model comparison showed a significant difference (see comments in the code below). Therefore, I now want to examine the partial metric measurement invariance. I want to remove the constraint, i.e. the equivalence of the loadings, for the first item (AIZ01_1 and AIZ01_2 should not be forced to have equal loadings). I tried this by using long.partial with the default longIndNames. Maybe I did something wrong here (I never worked with longIndNames before and I am calculating the partial invariance for the first time).

 I don't get any error message or warning, but the model comparison of the configural model with the metric model results in exactly the same output values as the comparison of the configural model with the partial metric model. This cannot be true! I therefore suspect that something went wrong when freeing the loadings of the first item between the two measurement points.

 I would be very pleased about a hint to this!

Here is my commented code:

   ##### Measurement Invariance of "Demands"

 ### Configural invariance

 model1 <- ' Demands_t1 =~ AIZ01_1 + AI02_1 + AI03_1

          Demands_t2 =~ AIZ01_2 + AI02_2 + AI03_2 '

 # Create list of variables

longFacNames <- list(Demands_both = c("Demands_t1","Demands_t2"))

 # Configural model: no constraints across repeated measures

syntax.config <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = model1, data = dataFS,

                               parameterization = "theta",

                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",

                               longFacNames = longFacNames)

 # Print a summary of model features

summary(syntax.config)

 # Fit a model to the data

mod.config <- as.character(syntax.config)

fit.config <- cfa(mod.config, data = dataFS, parameterization = "theta")

### Metric invariance

syntax.metric <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = model1, data = dataFS,

                               parameterization = "theta",

                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",

                               longFacNames = longFacNames,

                               long.equal  = c("loadings"))

 # Print a summary of model features

summary(syntax.metric)

# Fit model to data

mod.metric <- as.character(syntax.metric)

fit.metric <- cfa(mod.metric, data = dataFS, parameterization = "theta")

 # Compare model fits

compareFit(fit.config, fit.metric)

 # Result is: There is a significant difference between both models; thus, partial metric invariance shall be examined

### Partical metric invariance

 # Extract default longIndNames

syntax.metric@call$longIndNames

 # These are the longIndNames:

    #  $._Demands_both_.ind.1

    #  Demands_t1 Demands_t2

    #  "AIZ01_1"  "AIZ01_2"

    #  $._Demands_both_.ind.2

    #  Demands_t1 Demands_t2

    #  "AI02_1"   "AI02_2"

    #  $._Demands_both_.ind.3

    #  Demands_t1 Demands_t2

    #  "AI03_1"   "AI03_2"

# Constraint between "AIZ01_1" and "AIZ01_2" shall be freed --> "._Demands_both_.ind.1" is used in the long.partial argument

 syntax.metric.partial <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = model1, data = dataFS,

                               parameterization = "theta",

                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",

                               longFacNames = longFacNames,

                               long.equal  = c("loadings"), long.partial = c("._Demands_both_.ind.1 ~ 1"))

 # Print a summary of model features

summary(syntax.metric.partial)

 # Fit model to data

mod.metric.partial <- as.character(syntax.metric.partial)

fit.metric.partial <- cfa(mod.metric.partial, data = dataFS, parameterization = "theta")

 # Compare model fits

compareFit(fit.config, fit.metric.partial)

messages.subject: Re: factor scores calculation
messages.body_plain:
On 9/18/20 3:55 PM, Francesca Graziano wrote:
> I have a dataset with missing values and both binary and continous
> variable. I suppose there is one latent varaible underlying these. How
> can I calculate manually score using residual covariance matrix, factor
> loading matrix...

If your fitted object is called 'fit', then lavInspect(fit, "est") will
show all the (estimated) model matrices.

But it will not be trivial to compute the factor scores 'manually',
given that you have binary data. lavaan uses 'EBM' (Empirical Bayes
Modal) by default in this setting, and for each observation, the 'mode'
is found using numerical optimization. (ML is also available.)

The relevant code can be seen in the file 'lav_predict.R:

https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/blob/master/R/lav_predict.R

in the function 'lav_predict_eta_ebm_ml()' (starting from line 1018). A
local function is defined (f.eta.i, producing the loglikelihood of the
items, for given values of the factors), and nlminb() is used to find
the 'scores' (=values for the factors) that maximize this loglikelihood
(ML), or the posterior (EBM).

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: exact factorscores
messages.body_plain:
Luc

There are no "exact" factor scores, becuase any 1 set of factor scores is indeterminant. Meaning there can be multiple sets of factor scores that can satisfied ts conditions. To work with factor scores there is the still experimental method in lavaan, which is a 2 step method that adjust the factor scores to retain the factor relations between them. Or you could use the plausibel values approach to account for factor indeterminancy.

When you say that you dont want to have a Maximum Liklihood solution, and use VCOV. What are you looking for? What estimation method? Why you dont want to use ML? Sorry these thingas are not clear to me, and would help use to help you

With lavaan you can use different estimation methods, look the lavaan help page for more details, several of those adjust for non-normality, for categorical data, or with less assumptions. But ML would be the deault method, but you are not required to use it

messages.subject: Re: exact factorscores
messages.body_plain:
I also don't understand what you want. So, you have (somehow) computed
factor-scores F1, F2, ... Fn. And you wish to use them in a model, that
(I suppose) only contains regressions (as no measurement model is needed).

Then, you could use syntax like

model <- '

    F1 ~ F2 + F3 + F4
    F2 ~ F4
    # and so on
'

and fit the model with

fit <- sem(model, data = yourdata).

Indeed, by default lavaan will use ML estimation. But why is that a
problem? What is 'VCOV' referring to? The variance/covariance matrix of
the observed variables? Or the vcov of the parameter estimates?

Finally, factor scores still contain measurement error. To get
'unbiased' estimates (for the regression coefficients in the model
above), you can use Croon's correction. But for this, you need
information about the measurement models.

If you give us more context, we may help you better.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: exact factorscores
messages.body_plain:
Dear Mauga

I computed determinate factorscores using an alternating least squares method.
In any factor analysis you will find five matrices: Z, a centered datamatrix with unity length columns, U with the same order as Z, but consisting of the Unicities,   F , a matrix of factorscores, Labda wich is the loading matrix and psi, the diagonal matrix of standarddeviations of U.
in one simple equation:

Z =  F t(L) + U psi

Now estimate U by calculating a complete orthogonal matrix M with the smallest possible distance to Z. Use M to estimate U
Next , compute F by using any factorextraction.
Next , compute Labda as t(Z) F
Next , compute PSI just as  1 - Labda t(Labda)
You can iterate this by minimalising: U psi

The resulting F is a latent variable and an exact factorscore.
Just multiply F with (n - 1) / sqrt(n-1) and you get "conventional factorscores with standarddeviation of 1
My problem is the following : I created oblique ( coorelated) exact factoscores and to plug these into lavaan.
I definetely do not want to reinvent the wheel

messages.subject: Re: exact factorscores
messages.body_plain:
Not sure what you mean by "unity length." But factors are on an arbitrary metric, so you could use whatever SD you want. And SEM by design uses a variance-covariance matrix "under the hood." You haven't indicated why you wouldn't want that.

You also haven't told us your content area, but it's rarely going to be the case that important variables are perfectly orthogonal in any real-world setting, so I'd suggest using one of the oblique cases.

Frankly, you're not giving us a lot to work with to try to help.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: exact factorscores
messages.body_plain:
Luc

I have never seen the term "exact factor scores", any set of factor scores are approximations which can lead to issues.
The main ways to use factor scores and correct for this is eaither use the Croons corection or plausible vaues methods.
What you presented is one method to calculate the factor scores from a factor model, which would be similar to use a set of predicted factor scores from lavaan.
ALso, if you extract factor scores from an orthogonal model, and then do an alayis swith them, by default they will have 0 relations

As lavaan does SEM, it is a sufficient/limited information meaning that it will (by default) transformed the data set you provide into the variance/covariance matrix. And this matrix is used a the observed data for estimation. So, you can provide the factor scores matrix, or the covariance matrix between them. In any case lavaan wil end up using the same covariance matrix as it transform it before analysis.

It seems you are looking for a full information method that doesnt use sufficient/limited information. In lavaan you can do this with the estimator MML (Marginal Maximum Likelihood). There are other programs that will have other full information methods

-- Mauricio

messages.subject: Re: mediation analysis
messages.body_plain:
Adeela

You would need to include the IVs as predictors of the oitcome too, and include labels to estimate the indirect effects

IV1=~a1+a2+a3+a4+a5
IV2=~b1+b2+b3+b4+b5
IV3=~c1+c2+c3+c4+c5
IV4=~d1+d2+d3+d4+d5
M=~e1+e2+e3+e4+e5
O=~f1+f2+f3+f4+f5

M~ p1*IV1 + p2*IV2 + p3*IV3 + p4*IV4 + p5*IV5
O~ q1*M + cp1*IV1 + cp2*IV2 + cp3*IV3 + cp4*IV4 + cp5*IV5

## indirect effects
ind1 := p1*q1
ind2 := p2*q1
ind3 := p3*q1
ind4 := p4*q1
ind5 := p5*q1

Then you would need to use either bootstrap or monte carlo for the inference of the indirect effects

>
> IV1=~a1+a2+a3+a4+a5
> IV2=~b1+b2+b3+b4+b5

messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,

I've been having a lot of trouble getting lavaan to run these multigroup path models (attached below). Both the constrained and unconstrained outputs have df = 0, and are basically identical. This is weird because it's a very simple multivariate path model, with no latent variables or anything. However, I have no clue what could be going wrong with the code, since it appears to be specified correctly. Thanks so much for y'all's help!

model1<-'
yrelate~yreappt+yrsuppt+yage+ygender
yavoifu~yreappt+yrsuppt+yage+ygender
yanxtfu~yreappt+yrsuppt+yage+ygender'

#Specify Free Model.
multigroup <- sem(model1,data = merdata, group = "Dumsite_new")
summary(multigroup)

#Specify Constrained Model.
multigroup1.constrained <- sem(multigroup, data= merdata, group = "Dumsite_new", group.equal = c("regressions"))
summary(multigroup1.constrained)
anova(multigroup,multigroup1.constrained)

Hello Professor Terrence Jorgensen,

As I mentioned in a previous post, I need to perform an analysis of measurement invariance on a second-order model. I have already reviewed in detail the two papers you recommended and the help content for the measEq.syntax function. However, I have some difficulties.

When I evaluate the weak or metric invariance through the measEq.syntax function and set the factor loadings constraint using the group.equal = "loadings" argument, I get a result in which all coefficients are equal, not just the lambda, but also beta ones.

I suspect the above is not appropriate. As I understood it, it’s advisable to first test the invariance of the factor loadings in the first-order factors, and then do it in the second-order ones. I also think I understand that to do this with the measEq.syntax function, I must first use the "loadings" argument and then the "regressions" argument.

The same thing happens when I try to evaluate scalar or strong invariance. As recommended by Chen, Sousa and West (2005), first the equivalence must be analyzed by restricting the intercepts of the observed variables, and then testing this same level of invariance, but adding the intercepts of the latent variables. However, when I use the argument group.equal = c (“loadings”, “intercepts”), once again, all intercepts are equal.

I would like to know how I can constrain only one type of parameter at a time; that is, first restrict only the factor loadings, leaving the regression coefficients to be freely estimated, and then restrict both parameters. And the same with the intercepts, but also with the residual variance and the disturbance.

How can I fix this problem? I have tried modifying the syntax that the measEq.syntax function generates but not succeeded. I have a hard time understanding how the syntax works. On the other hand, would it be correct to compare the models in which factor loadings and regression coefficients are restricted at the same time with the previous configural model? Can I proceed in this way with the other levels of invariance?

Here are my codes and results

#DEFINING THE MODEL
MSPSS_Model <- '
F1 =~ a1+a2+a5+a10
F2 =~ a3+a4+a8+a11
F3 =~ a6+a7+a9+a12
F4 =~ F1+F2+F3'

#EVALUATING METRIC INVARIANCE CONSTRAINING FIRST-ORDER FACTOR LOADINGS
syntax00 <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = MSPSS_Model, estimator = "MLR", ID.fac = "UL", group = "sex", group.equal = "loadings)
Model05 <- as.character(syntax00)
summary(syntax00)
cat(Model05)
fit05 <- cfa(Model05, data = MSPSS_DB, estimator = "MLR", group = "sex")
summary(fit05, fit.measures = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Professors,

I am doing a mediation analysis within latent growth curve model, and  I continuouly got one error message and don't know how to deal with it. Briefly, I introduce my analyses and database first. My analyses is to look at how variable "m" relate to a distal outcome, whether there exist direct effect or indirect effect mediated by variable "r".  My study is a longitudinal design, therefore, variable "m" and variable "r" were measured repeatly at 5 time points. In addition, there are several time-invariant covariates, such as sex, and the distal outcome is a binary variable, coded as 0 for no outcome and 1 for having the outcome. messages.subject: Re: How can I construct single-indicator latent variable model?
messages.subject_clean: How can I construct single-indicator latent variable model?
messages.body_plain:
> I fix the coefficient of the C1 at one and error variance of it

C1 is ordinal, so its (error) variance is not modeled.  The variance of its latent response (assumed normal) is assumed 1 by default (parameterization = "delta"), and its error variance is simply 1 minus the variance explained by the common factor.  Because f3 is not a common factor (only a single indicator), you don't have enough information to identify its variance.  So specifying a single ordinal indicator would be accomplished by using parameterization = "theta" (so the error variances are model parameters instead of the scales of the latent item responses), in which case all indicators are identified by fixing their error variances to 1.  Thus, you would fix the single-indicator's error variance to zero and its factor variance to one, if you assumed the single indicator were without measurement error.

To account for unreliability of the indicator, you would fix the error variance to 1 - alpha instead of zero, and fix the factor variance to alpha instead of 1.

> #Raw Cronbach's alpha is 0.783 and var is 0.957
> C1 ~~ (1-0.783)*0.957*C1

Actually do the math, so you can put the fixed values in the syntax.

C1 ~~ 0.217*C1
f3 ~~ 0.783*f3

messages.subject: Re: Problems with reproducing results for a measurement invariance test
messages.subject_clean: Problems with reproducing results for a measurement invariance test
messages.body_plain:
Analyzing longitudinal data as multigroup data ignores the dependence among observations.  The dependence is represented in the covariances among variables across occasions in a longitudinal model.  You are not fitting the same model to the same data (i.e., 324 observed between-time covariances between 3 variables across 9 occasions disappear), and you should not treat occasions as independent groups.

FYI, there is a longInvariance() function (also deprecated) that would be more appropriate for your situation.  There is also a measEq.syntax() function that is much more pedagogically useful, as the whole point is that it writes syntax you can inspect.  The first help-page example has a longitudinal (2-occasion) model, as well as 2 groups, but you can ignore the group arguments and just adapt it to your 9-occasion example.

messages.subject: Re: Error message in measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
> When I evaluate the weak or metric invariance through the measEq.syntax function and set the factor loadings constraint using the group.equal = "loadings" argument, I get a result in which all coefficients are equal, not just the lambda, but also beta ones.

No, your syntax doesn't do that.  Your syntax doesn't even know that there are multiple groups, because you supplied the group= argument without supplying the data= in which to find it.  So measEq.syntax() returned syntax for a siingle-group model, which is why you only see one label and one value (or NA) for each parameter.  You can supply data, or you can at least pass a vector of sample sizes to indicate the number of groups (see below), although that second option is only available in the development version.

Because your syntax has only one label per parameter, lavaan recycles that label for all groups, so all parameters (not just loadings) are constrained to equality.  But measEq.syntax() will return correct syntax for separately constrained first- and second-order loadings if it knows there are multiple groups.  Here is a reproducible example:

HS.higher <- '
visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
intel   =~ visual + textual + speed
'
syntax.hi <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = HS.higher,
                           sample.nobs = c(1,1), # two indicate 2 groups without data
                           group.equal = "loadings")
cat(as.character(syntax.hi))
summary(syntax.hi)

Notice that the higher-order loadings will have the same parameter label except for the ".g1" or ".g2" suffix for different groups.

Glad my function is helping to execute the methods you read about,

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> > When I evaluate the weak or metric invariance through the measEq.syntax function and set the factor loadings constraint using the group.equal = "loadings" argument, I get a result in which all coefficients are equal, not just the lambda, but also beta ones.
>
> No, your syntax doesn't do that.  Your syntax doesn't even know that there are multiple groups, because you supplied the group= argument without supplying the data= in which to find it.  So measEq.syntax() returned syntax for a siingle-group model, which is why you only see one label and one value (or NA) for each parameter.  You can supply data, or you can at least pass a vector of sample sizes to indicate the number of groups (see below), although that second option is only available in the development version.
>
> Because your syntax has only one label per parameter, lavaan recycles that label for all groups, so all parameters (not just loadings) are constrained to equality.  But measEq.syntax() will return correct syntax for separately constrained first- and second-order loadings if it knows there are multiple groups.  Here is a reproducible example:
>
> HS.higher <- '
> visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
> textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
> speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
> intel   =~ visual + textual + speed
> '
> syntax.hi <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = HS.higher,
>                            sample.nobs = c(1,1), # two indicate 2 groups without data
>                            group.equal = "loadings")
> cat(as.character(syntax.hi))
> summary(syntax.hi)
>
> Notice that the higher-order loadings will have the same parameter label except for the ".g1" or ".g2" suffix for different groups.
>

messages.subject: Re: Error message in measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
> What arguments should I use to constrain the disturbances associated to the second-order factors? As far as I know, the residuals argument allows to constrain the residual variance of measured variables, but what option do I use in the case of latent variables?

"lv.variances" will constrain variances of all latent variables, both residual variances of latent indicators and exogenous variances of higher-order factors.  You can use the group.partial= argument to free the higher-order factor variance, in order to constrain only the residual variances of first-order indicators.  I noted this strategy with respect to latent intercepts in the help-page Details: "To test equivalence of lower-order and higher-order intercepts/means in separate steps, the user can either manually edit their generated syntax or conscientiously exploit the group.partial or long.partial arguments as necessary", in case that also becomes relevant for you.

> How do I get the test for the difference in the robust chi-squared statistics?  When I use the anova or compareFit option, the results are based in the standard statistics, but I need the robust scaled version from Satorra-Bentler.

If you requested it when fitting the model (either using estimator = "MLM" or test = "satorra.bentler"), then the difference between (naive) chi-squared statistics will be scaled using the S-B method.  This should be stated explicitly at the top of the anova() output, which also appears at the top of the nested-model comparisons part of the compareFit() output.  Here are details about how the robust chi-squared difference test is calculated:

https://www.statmodel.com/chidiff.shtml

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> So my questions are, (1) I cannot use the cluster option in this
> mediation model?

The cluster option is only available for continuous data, not for
categorical data. That also explains the error message.

If you have family data, the number of observations (per family) is
usually small. I would suggest to reshape your data to 'wide-format', so
that you have a single line per family. That will allow you to use
categorical data, and estimators like WLSMV.

A paper about this approach can be found here:

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1689366

Yves.

Il giorno mercoledì 23 settembre 2020 alle 08:51:06 UTC+2 yros...@gmail.com ha scritto:
> On 9/18/20 3:55 PM, Francesca Graziano wrote:
> > I have a dataset with missing values and both binary and continous
> > variable. I suppose there is one latent varaible underlying these. How
> > can I calculate manually score using residual covariance matrix, factor
> > loading matrix...
>
> If your fitted object is called 'fit', then lavInspect(fit, "est") will
> show all the (estimated) model matrices.
>
> But it will not be trivial to compute the factor scores 'manually',
> given that you have binary data. lavaan uses 'EBM' (Empirical Bayes
> Modal) by default in this setting, and for each observation, the 'mode'
> is found using numerical optimization. (ML is also available.)
>
> The relevant code can be seen in the file 'lav_predict.R:
>
> https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/blob/master/R/lav_predict.R
>
> in the function 'lav_predict_eta_ebm_ml()' (starting from line 1018). A
> local function is defined (f.eta.i, producing the loglikelihood of the
> items, for given values of the factors), and nlminb() is used to find
> the 'scores' (=values for the factors) that maximize this loglikelihood
> (ML), or the posterior (EBM).
>
> Yves.

messages.subject_clean: lavaan WARNING: syntax contains parameters involving exogenous covariates; switching to fixed.x = FALSE
messages.body_plain:
Typically in SEM, exogenous variables are treated differently in the estimation process from endogenous variables. By explicity specifying their covariances, you are "bringing them into" the model and lavaan treats them in the same way as it does endogenous variables. So the usual practice is not to have a section like "# Exogenous predictors correlations." It's also usually not necessary--all exogenous covariables are free to covary by default.

However, before that section, you have this:
beta ~~ SizeInvDis.3   + SizeInvDis.9   + SizeInvDis.15   + SizeInvDis.21   +
        Breastfed.3    + Breastfed.9    + Breastfed.15    + Breastfed.21    +
        ChildHealth.3  + ChildHealth.9  + ChildHealth.15  + ChildHealth.21  +
        FS.score.0     + FS.score.6     + FS.score.12     + FS.score.18     +
        MotherHealth.0 + MotherHealth.6 + MotherHealth.12 + MotherHealth.18 +
        LnExpenditure.0

Which brings them into the model. It also has causes of the indicators of beta correlate with beta--is that what you want? If it is, then yes, you do need that other section, and the warning is letting you know lavaan adapted appropriately to your specification--note that is a warning, not an error. Was the model identified?

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Dear Coding Engineers,

I am currently working on sample size calculation via R package 'simsem' for a CFA-based questionnaire validation project. To emphasize, this is a social science research.
(Pornprasertmanit Miller, Schoemann, Jorgensen, 2020)
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/simsem/simsem.pdf

To provide context for my model:
My model is a latent model; 3 Latent Variables,

Indicators and Latent Variable
3 Indicators for two Latent Variables and the last Latent Variable with 4.
Hence, Total of 3 Latent and 10 Measured Variables.

Paramaratization nature of CFA model:
Two latent variables are correlated with each other,
while the last latent variable is negatively correlated both of the other two.

All indicator / measured variables are expected to positively estimate unto their respective latent variables.

In R, my model should look like this
X =~ x1 + x2 + x3
Y =~ y1 + y2 + y3
Z =~ z1 + z2 + z3 + z4

X ~~ Y
Z ~~ Y

In terms of conceptual framework, you may look at the attached file below for clarification.

I will run through my attempt using an example broken down into components as a template from this link and also provide some questions for those I have no idea how to deal with :
https://rdrr.io/cran/simsem/man/continuousPower.html

Full Example
# Specify Sample Size by n
loading <- matrix(0, 6, 1)
loading[1:6, 1] <- NA
LY <- bind(loading, 0.7)
RPS <- binds(diag(1))
RTE <- binds(diag(6))
CFA.Model <- model(LY = LY, RPS = RPS, RTE = RTE, modelType="CFA")
dat <- generate(CFA.Model, 50)
out <- analyze(CFA.Model, dat)

# Specify both continuous sample size and percent missing completely at random.
# Note that more fine-grained values of n and pmMCAR is needed, e.g., n=seq(50, 500, 1)
# and pmMCAR=seq(0, 0.2, 0.01)
Output <- sim(NULL, CFA.Model, n=seq(100, 200, 20), pmMCAR=c(0, 0.1, 0.2))
summary(Output)

# Find the power of all combinations of different sample size and percent MCAR missing
Cpow <- continuousPower(Output, contN = TRUE, contMCAR = TRUE)
Cpow

# Find the power of parameter estimates when sample size is 200 and percent MCAR missing is 0.3
Cpow2 <- continuousPower(Output, contN = TRUE, contMCAR = TRUE, pred=list(N = 200, pmMCAR = 0.3))
Cpow2

Example 1#
# Specify Sample Size by n
loading <- matrix(0, 6, 1)
loading[1:6, 1] <- NA

My Coding 1#
loading <- matrix(0, 10, 3)
loading[1:3, 1] <- NA
loading[4:6, 2] <- NA
loading[7:10, 3] <- NA

Question (1)
What does NA indicates?

Question (2)
What about covariance?

I found one simulation that specify it around:
#Specify latent variances and covariances
latent.cor <- matrix(NA, 2, 2)
diag(latent.cor) <- 1
RPH <- symMatrix(latent.cor, 0.1)

#Specify measurement errors
error.cor <- matrix(0, 6, 6)
diag(error.cor) <- 1
RTD <- symMatrix(error.cor)
https://github.com/simsem/simsem/blob/master/Conference%20presentations/IMPS_simsem.R

Question (3)
How do I identify and apply relevant matrix and diag settings?

Example 2#
LY <- bind(loading, 0.7)
RPS <- binds(diag(1))
RTE <- binds(diag(6))

My Coding 2#
I have no idea how to deal with this.

Example 3#
CFA.Model <- model(LY = LY, RPS = RPS, RTE = RTE, modelType="CFA")
dat <- generate(CFA.Model, 50)
out <- analyze(CFA.Model, dat)

My Coding 3#
CFA.Model <- model(LY=LY, RPS=RPS, RTE=RTE, modelType="CFA")
dat <- generate(CFA.Model, 50)
out <- analyze(CFA.Model, dat)

Question (4)
For
"dat <- generate(CFA.Model, 50)"

The 50 above is the sample size that I want to simulate for power analysis.
Is this interpretation correct?
If I am correct, should 50 be the default number? or should there be some condition or assumptions to look for?

Example 4#
# Specify both continuous sample size and percent missing completely at random.
# Note that more fine-grained values of n and pmMCAR is needed, e.g., n=seq(50, 500, 1)
# and pmMCAR=seq(0, 0.2, 0.01)

Output <- sim(NULL, CFA.Model, n=seq(100, 200, 20), pmMCAR=c(0, 0.1, 0.2))
summary(Output)

My Coding 4#

summary(Output)

Example 5#
# Find the power of all combinations of different sample size and percent MCAR missing
Cpow <- continuousPower(Output, contN = TRUE, contMCAR = TRUE)
Cpow

My Coding 5#

Cpow

Example 6#

Cpow2 <- continuousPower(Output, contN = TRUE, contMCAR = TRUE, pred=list(N = 200, pmMCAR = 0.3))

Cpow2

My Coding 6#

Question (5)
Is there a wiki/book that summarize all the NULL, TRUE interpretation for all of the functions above?

Thanks,
Brandon

messages.subject: How to run CFA or SEM in LAVAAN when Indicator Variables for measuring the Latent Variables are binary categorical
messages.subject_clean: How to run CFA or SEM in LAVAAN when Indicator Variables for measuring the Latent Variables are binary categorical
messages.body_plain:
Dear LAVAAN community

I am struggling with the following issue.
For the measurement of the latent variables, the indicators variables that I am using are all binary categorical variables having two levels (0 for no, and 1 for yes).
For instance, for measuring X =~ x1+ x2+ x3 (all the xi take either of the two values: 0/1). And as per my understanding, the default measure in LAVAAN is MLE which is for continuous indicator variables. So when I run the SEM command, I am getting different warning messages and the model is not running accurately.
I looked at various places and there are suggestions like keeping the value of categorical indicator variables in numeric terms (like 1,2,3) will work but apparently it is not. further I checked that the degrees of freedom are positive so there should not be a problem of identification which might be generating warning messages.

Can anyone please take out some time and help me out in this. I have been struggling and have spent a lot of time but could not find a solution. The examples and explanations given everywhere is either about continuous variables or about the ordered argument in the SEM function (which is also not working for me).

Regards
Priya

messages.body_plain:
Priya,

Positive degrees of freedom means you don't have a certain type of identification problem, but a model can also be locally unidentified. One of the places this often happens is a factor with rare categorical indicators.

It's hard to help more without more information. What is your model? If your model is large, please post a small version that still causes the problem. What is your sem() call? What is the exact language of the warnings you are getting? Are they warnings or errors? Warnings don't necessarily invalidate your results, though you should certainly consider them and why you're getting them.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Priya,

Thanks for the additional information.

Let's start with the first error:

missing observed variables in dataset: f_tv f_smart_phone f_computer f_open_read_sms  f_mobile_banking
 f_online_phone_apps

It tells you what the problem is. These newly created variables aren't in the dataframe eth.

Instead of:

f_tv <- factor(tv, levels = c("0", "1"), ordered = TRUE)

try

eth$f_tv <- factor(eth$tv, levels = c("0", "1"), ordered = TRUE)

That will put the new variable into eth so it will be available to cfa().

Also, one of your attempts resulted in:

WARNING: ordered variable(s): ICT_access ICT_capability
  could not be found in the data and will be ignored

ICT_access and ICT_capability aren't in the eth dataset because they're latent variables you're estimating from the observed variables. (Also, even with ordered indicators, the latents aren't ordered, butthat's a different issue.)

Hope that helps.

Pat

# Measurement model
e.g., X1 =~ x1a + x1b + x1c

e.g., Med1a ~ a*X1 + *X2
...
# Residual correlations
X1 ~~ X2
DV1 ~~ 0*DV2

# Defined parameters (indirect effects)
e.g., indirecteffect1 := a*c
...

For the 'Residual correlations', what I noticed was that if I do not set DV1 ~~ 0*DV2, lavaan computes the association between two final, endogenous variables.

I was wondering if this is something run by default in lavaan.

messages.body_plain:
> I don't see the E part in the equation

Every variable has a disturbance term.  Residuals are thus referred to by the name of its associated variable.  For example, the residual variance of q1a is specified as:

q1a ~~ q1a

You can automatically free all (residual) variances using the option auto.var=TRUE, which is already turned on by default in the sem() and cfa() wrappers around the basic lavaan() function.

> Question (1)
> What does NA indicates?

That indicates "missing value" in R.  In simsem, a missing parameter is one that is not fixed to a specific value, so it is estimated. > Question (2)
> What about covariance?
>

> Question (3)

> Question (4)
> For
> "dat <- generate(CFA.Model, 50)"
>
> The 50 above is the sample size that I want to simulate for power analysis.
> Is this interpretation correct?

You can find a description of each argument on the ?generate help page.

> If I am correct, should 50 be the default number? or should there be some condition or assumptions to look for?

Depends on context.  As you next line of syntax indicates, the point of this example is to vary N so that power can be estimated at different Ns.

> Question (5)
> Is there a wiki/book that summarize all the NULL, TRUE interpretation for all of the functions above?

You can read the help page for whatever function you are asking about, and the vignettes (especially early ones) explain much about the package:  https://github.com/simsem/simsem/wiki/Vignette

Further, there's excellent reason for that to be the default in lavaan (as Terrence said, "makes sense to free"), as it is in most software I have used. In most practical situations, that would be quite a strong declaration.

messages.body_plain:
A colleague pointed me towards the following thread https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/JO5pr0fj5TY/m/AZw6722VKbwJ for a problem I had (it was similar to the one posted in 2014 I refer to): in order to test for mediation, I had to bootstrap the SE's. I was also using 'ordered' data and, for similar reasons, was using the WLSMV estimator. Using the WLSMV estimator, however, was/is not possible when using bootstrapping.

The post offered a suggestion, but I run into the problem that roughly 1 in 10 draws the result fails to converge. Now, this is not necessarily my problem, but lavaan seems to stop the process well before the number of draws I ask to be drawn. So far i have managed to reach 291 draws.

Do I have options? I would very much like to be able to bootstrap the SE's using the WLSMV estimator. The above suggestion of adding test="scaled.shifted", seems a step in the right direction, but lavaan simply stops (I assume it is related to these unsuccessful draws?). Is there, however a way to 'force' lavaan to continue? I'd prefer to have at least 1000 successful draws.

Further information:
I am using lavaan 0.6-7 and I ran the following command:
MedAppCtrlBoot2.fit <- sem(MedAppCtrl.sem,
                          CsetNorm,
                          se = "bootstrap",
                          test = "scaled.shifted",
                          bootstrap = 5000,
                          parallel = "multicore",
                          ncpus=16,
                          estimator = "DWLS",
                          verbose= TRUE
)
summary(MedAppCtrlBoot2.fit, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
parameterEstimates(MedAppCtrlBoot2.fit, standardized=TRUE)

PS. I have also tried the above without using parallel processing. No difference. I just hoped to speed up matters.

Thank you very much for any help.

messages.body_plain:
To add to the discussion, simsem can use either the matrix style input (as you're using above) or lavaan syntax as input for models. If you're running through a lot of conditions and changing parameter values often, using the matrix style input is easier. But if you're just running simulations for small models, with a limited set of parameter values it's probably easier to use lavaan syntax as input. On the vignette page (https://github.com/simsem/simsem/wiki/Vignette) be sure to look at the lavaan syntax specification examples

Alex

messages.subject: Re: Setting bootstrap in sem() and/or parameterEstimates()
messages.subject_clean: Setting bootstrap in sem() and/or parameterEstimates()
messages.body_plain:
1. When setting bootstrap, I noticed that the results differ when:

The bootstrap is set early on when fitting the model

fit=sem(model, data, se="bootstrap", bootstrap=5000)
and then, running parameterEstimates(fit, level=0.95, boot.ci.type="bca.simple")

In this case you are looking at standard error and CI based on the 5000 bootstrap you asked

OR, the bootstrap is set when estimating the parameter, where

fit=sem(model, data)
parameterEstimates(fit, level=0.95, boot.ci.type="bca.simple")

In this case you are seeing results based on the Wlad tests, no boostrap has be asked. You need to include the arguments se="bootstrap", bootstrap=5000in the sem funtion to get bootstrap results

Are both of these approaches correct?

Only the first is actually doing boostrap

2. Another question I had was for boot.ci.type, is there a way to get standard errors for bootstrapping based on percentile method (rather than bootstrapping and accelerated)?

Specified boot.ci.type = "perc" in the parameterestimates function, this will give you results based on the percentile boostrap

messages.subject: Re: # of succesful bootstraps = 0 when I increase the total number of bootstraps?
messages.subject_clean: # of succesful bootstraps = 0 when I increase the total number of bootstraps?
messages.body_plain:
One option might be to use a different method of testing the indirect effect. A Monte Carlo confidence interval (see http://quantpsy.org/pubs/preacher_selig_2012.pdf for details) will allow you to accurately and powerfully test the indirect effect without bootstrapping. If you're interested in this approach the monteCarloMed function in semTools works with lavaan objects to create Monte Carlo confidence intervals for any combination of parameters (I'm not 100% sure it works with WLS, but if not please let me know and we'll fix that).

It's impossible to know exactly what the issue is with bootstrapping here, but if I had to guess I'd say it's likely due to either missing data (resulting in so much missing data for a bootstrap sample the model isn't estimable), or some categories with small frequencies (so in some bootstrap samples a variable is a constant).

Alex

messages.body_plain:
I would not trust standard errors if you are getting 291 usable replicates out of 5,000. Something is very bad with your combination of the model, the data, and the estimator. If you have 0/1 variables where only 3% of observations are positive/1 and 97% are negative/0, then your data are so skewed that the asymptotic assumptions underlying both the ADF as the estimation method and the bootstrap as the concept really need tens of thousands of cases for it to work well.

messages.subject: chi square difference test WLSMV
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Can anyone help me with this? How can I run a chi-square difference test for two nested models fitted with WLSMV from lavaan's fitMeasures() output?

Would it be valid to take this approach: https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/mplus/faq/how-can-i-compute-a-chi-square-test-for-nested-models-with-the-mlr-or-mlm-estimators/

which does the following:

c0 = scaling correction factor for the null model.
c1 = scaling correction factor for the alternative model.

d0 = degrees of freedom for the null model.
d1 = degrees of freedom for the alternative model.

SB0 = Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square value for the null model.
SB1 = Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square value for the alternative model.
In order to calculate the test statistic, T, we first need to calculate the value cd:

cd = (d0 * c0 - d1 * c1)/(d0 - d1)
Once we have calculated cd, we can compute:

T = (SB0 * c0 - SB1 * c1)/cd
T is distributed chi-square with degrees of freedom:

df = d0 - d1

>From lavaan's fitMeasures output, which one is the Satorra-Bentler chi-square? Is it simply the one that says "chisq.scaled"?

I cannot do this in lavaan directly, because I only have the estimated parameters and the goodness of fit measures.

Any advice would be very highly appreciated!

Thanks!

P

If you use the default nested model compariosn function in lavaan lavTestLRT (or the anova() function ), when comparisng models ran with WLS, they will be compared with the Sattorra adjusted method. Lavaan does this for you automatically.

Like in thid example, you an see it says that its doing the Satoora.2000 by default for WLS models, but you can choose other methods

HS.model <- '
    visual  =~ x1 + b1*x2 + x3
    textual =~ x4 + b2*x5 + x6
    speed   =~ x7 + b3*x8 + x9
'
fit1 <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
            estimator="wlsmv")
fit0 <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
            estimator="wlsmv",orthogonal = TRUE)

On Tuesday, September 29, 2020 at 12:05:52 PM UTC+2 ptronruin wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> Can anyone help me with this? How can I run a chi-square difference test for two nested models fitted with WLSMV from lavaan's fitMeasures() output?
>
> Would it be valid to take this approach: https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/mplus/faq/how-can-i-compute-a-chi-square-test-for-nested-models-with-the-mlr-or-mlm-estimators/
>
> which does the following:
>
> c0 = scaling correction factor for the null model.
> c1 = scaling correction factor for the alternative model.
>
> d0 = degrees of freedom for the null model.
> d1 = degrees of freedom for the alternative model.
>
> SB0 = Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square value for the null model.
> SB1 = Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square value for the alternative model.
> In order to calculate the test statistic, T, we first need to calculate the value cd:
>
> cd = (d0 * c0 - d1 * c1)/(d0 - d1)
> Once we have calculated cd, we can compute:
>
> T = (SB0 * c0 - SB1 * c1)/cd
> T is distributed chi-square with degrees of freedom:
>
> df = d0 - d1
>
> From lavaan's fitMeasures output, which one is the Satorra-Bentler chi-square? Is it simply the one that says "chisq.scaled"?
>
> I cannot do this in lavaan directly, because I only have the estimated parameters and the goodness of fit measures.
>
> Any advice would be very highly appreciated!
>
> Thanks!
>
> P

messages.subject: Re: Difference between robust.cluster and robust.cluster.sem
messages.body_plain:
On 9/29/20 7:23 AM, h.park wrote:
> Dear experts,
>
> I was just wondering what the difference is between the
> robust.cluster and the robust.cluster.sem options for producing
> standard errors for a model that contains clustered data?

The distinction is similar to the (estimator) mlm vs mlr difference. The
former uses the classic formulas to compute 'robust' standard errors as
described in the SEM literature (robust.sem), while the latter uses the
'Huber-White' (or sandwich) formulas (robust.huber.white). Another way
of looking a this is that the default settings for specifying the
'bread' and the 'meat' of the sandwich formula is slightly different in
the two variants. But the results are often very similar (or indeed
identical).

This is (an old) document about it:

https://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/utrecht2010.pdf

The 'cluster' version simply extends these two variants to produce
cluster-robust standard errors.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Mauricio and Yves!

I think I've just made a rooky mistake!

By following Yves's suggestion of A.method="exact", I could see that the problems was that in the eyes of lavaan my models weren't nested.

I hadn't specified the baseline model with the additional parameters fixed to 0.

I'm leaving this here in case someone else makes the same mistake. So, this is what I had done (borrowing from Mauricio's example):

m0 <- '
    visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 +  x4
    textual =~ x5+ x6 + x7 +  x8
    speed   =~ x8 + x9 + x10
'
m1 <- '
    visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 +  x4
    textual =~ x5+ x6 + x7 +  x8
    speed   =~ x8 + x9 + x10 + x11
'
lavTestLRT(m0, m1)

Error!

This is what I should've done:

m0b <- '
    visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 +  x4
    textual =~ x5+ x6 + x7 +  x8
    speed   =~ x8 + x9 + x10 + 0*x11
'
m1b <- '
    visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 +  x4
    textual =~ x5+ x6 + x7 +  x8
    speed   =~ x8 + x9 + x10 + x11
'

lavTestLRT(m0b, m1b)

m0 is statistically equivalent to m0b, but it needs to be specified in the latter way for difftest to work. I know this is probably obvious to most of you, but it wasn't to me.

Thanks for your help and apologies for the silly mistake!

P

messages.subject: Re: Error message in measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
Dear Professor Terrence,

I hope you are well.

I am bothering you again for a question related to an CFA. When I run the following syntax everything works fine, except for the last result. I get this error message when executing this command:

> compareFit (original.fit04, original.fit03, original.fit02, original.fit01)
Error in svd (X): a dimension is zero

This is the code I used:

Casullo.original <- '
CTRL =~ b1+b5+b10+b13
VINC =~ b2+b8+b11
PROY =~ b3+b6+b12
ACEP =~ b4+b7+b9'

original.syntax01 <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = Casullo.original, data = CasulloDB, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", group = "sex", parameterization = "theta")

original.syntax02 <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = Casullo.original, data = CasulloDB, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",  group = "sex", group.equal = "loadings", parameterization = "theta")

original.syntax03 <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = Casullo.original, data = CasulloDB, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",  group = "sex", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"), parameterization = "theta")

original.syntax04 <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = Casullo.original, data = CasulloDB, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",  group = "sex", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals"), parameterization = "theta")

original.configural <- as.character(original.syntax01)
original.metric <- as.character(original.syntax02)
original.scalar <- as.character(original.syntax03)
original.strict <- as.character(original.syntax04)

cat(original.configural)
cat(original.metric)
cat(original.scalar)
car(original.strict)

original.fit01 <- cfa(original.configural, data = CasulloDB, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "sex")
original.fit02 <- cfa(original.metric, data = CasulloDB, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "sex")
original.fit03 <- cfa(original.scalar, data = CasulloDB, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "sex")
original.fit04 <- cfa(original.strict, data = CasulloDB, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", group = "sex")

compareFit(original.fit04, original.fit03, original.fit02, original.fit01)

I would greatly appreciate your help again. Thanks in advance. Greetings.

El jue., 24 sept. 2020 a las 14:24, Juan Diego Hernández Lalinde (<hernandez...@gmail.com>) escribió:
> Thanks a lot, professor.
>
> El jue., 24 de septiembre de 2020 13:57, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> escribió:
> > > What arguments should I use to constrain the disturbances associated to the second-order factors? As far as I know, the residuals argument allows to constrain the residual variance of measured variables, but what option do I use in the case of latent variables?
> >
> > "lv.variances" will constrain variances of all latent variables, both residual variances of latent indicators and exogenous variances of higher-order factors.  You can use the group.partial= argument to free the higher-order factor variance, in order to constrain only the residual variances of first-order indicators.  I noted this strategy with respect to latent intercepts in the help-page Details: "To test equivalence of lower-order and higher-order intercepts/means in separate steps, the user can either manually edit their generated syntax or conscientiously exploit the group.partial or long.partial arguments as necessary", in case that also becomes relevant for you.
> >
> > > How do I get the test for the difference in the robust chi-squared statistics?  When I use the anova or compareFit option, the results are based in the standard statistics, but I need the robust scaled version from Satorra-Bentler.
> >
> > If you requested it when fitting the model (either using estimator = "MLM" or test = "satorra.bentler"), then the difference between (naive) chi-squared statistics will be scaled using the S-B method.  This should be stated explicitly at the top of the anova() output, which also appears at the top of the nested-model comparisons part of the compareFit() output.  Here are details about how the robust chi-squared difference test is calculated:

messages.subject: Re: Plotting latent interaction
messages.body_plain:
To answer your questions:

1. I'm not sure why you want to have the outcome on the x axis and the predictor on the y axis. Almost every plot of two variables includes the outcome (Y variable) on the y axis and predictor (X variable) on the x axis. If you really want to change things, the output from probe2WayMC should give you the simple intercepts and slopes, with an intercept and slope you can then plot a line in any number of plotting packages/software.

2. Pick the values that are meaningful. There's no rule that says which values you need to pick. With a latent moderator the default is +-1 SD since the metric of the latent variable isn't meaningful. With age you would pick the values that are most relevant.
